title: Show HN: I turned 18 Agatha Christie novels into SQL murder cases
author: jenikashah07
body:
Start Investigation 
Learn SQL by solving murder mysteries
Query the Murder is a free SQL game built around Agatha Christie mysteries. Every case comes with a real database of suspects, alibis and evidence. You write SQL queries to check the alibis, follow the clues and name the killer.
There are 18 cases. The early ones teach SELECT and WHERE. Later cases bring in JOINs, GROUP BY, subqueries and window functions. No account needed.
How it works
Pick a case. Each one is based on an Agatha Christie novel, from Murder on the Orient Express to Endless Night.
Read the case brief and explore the tables of suspects, alibis and events.
Answer 5 questions by writing SQL. Each question teaches you something new.
Solve the last question to name the killer and close the case.

title: Show HN: Exact integer LLL lattice basis reduction in C99
author: qawbecrdtey
body:
LLL, also known as Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász lattice basis reduction algorithm, is an important algorithm in mathematics and cryptography.
clll is an implementation of LLL in C99, which is small, is based on formally verified algorithm, and uses integer arithmetic only (GMP).Claim. clll is also high performant, based on the private benchmarks I have run comparing LLL implementations with exact arithmetic.

Do I need a household to use Cinnamon?

title: Show HN: Amigent – AI agent and remote desktop for Commodore Amiga over 50 KB/s
author: akustikrausch
body:
# akustikrausch/amigent

Complete remote control for a real Amiga, by AI or manually: an MCP server for AI agents and a remote desktop like TeamViewer, tuned for slow Amigas and slow networks. AmigaOS 2.04 and up, any CPU from the 68000, Windows, macOS and Linux.

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-02T00:56:09Z

## Languages

- C
- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Python
- REXX
- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- ai-agent
- amiga

- amigaos
- amigaos3
- claude-code

- commodore-amiga

## Top Contributors

- akustikrausch (139 contributions)

---

## README

```
     _____            .__                            __
    /  _  \    _____  |__|   ____    ____    ____  _/  |_
   /  /_\  \  /     \ |  |  / ___\ _/ __ \  /    \ \   __\
  /    |    \|  Y Y  \|  | / /_/  >\  ___/ |   |  \ |  |
  \____|__  /|__|_|  /|__| \___  /  \___  >|___|  / |__|
          \/       \/     /_____/       \/      \/

     complete remote control for a real Amiga, by AI or manually
            tuned for slow Amigas and slow networks
```

 

Amigent connects your PC or Mac to your real Amiga over the home network. Then you can:

- **let an AI agent do the work**, for example Claude Code or Codex: install
 software, update programs, change settings, copy files, click through
 programs. Just tell it what you want.
- **use the Amiga yourself from your computer**, as a remote desktop like
 TeamViewer or VNC: a window with the live screen, your own mouse and
 keyboard, file transfer and a shared clipboard.
- **and both of these quickly, even on a slow machine.** Amigent is tuned for
 slow Amigas and slow networks: a 7 MHz 68000 sends its whole screen in
 under a second, and over a plipbox a click shows its result in a fraction of a second.
 How it stays fast.

Both at the same time: you see every click the agent makes and can take over at
any moment.

Amigent with a Workbench screen and the keyboard panel

## Installation

### On the Amiga

**1.** Copy `amigentd` to the Amiga (`amigentd.000` on a
68000), or unpack the archive from the
releases.

**2.** Start it with `amigentd SETUP` in a Shell, or double-click its icon.

### On the PC or Mac

**3.** Paste this into your AI agent:

 Install Amigent for me: run "pipx install amigent" (if pipx or Python 3.10
 or newer is missing, install them first: Windows winget, macOS Homebrew,
 Linux the package manager). Then run amigent-setup; it finds my Amiga on
 the network by itself. Register the MCP server "amigent" with the command
 amigent-server, and run amigent-viewer --install so the remote desktop
 shows up as a program. Tell me if you need to be restarted.

The agent sets up the Amiga over the network; from then on amigentd starts
with it.

**Windows:** Amigent appears in the Start menu. For an encrypted connection
`openssl` is needed, which comes with Git for Windows.

**macOS:** Amigent appears in `~/Applications`. On its first start, allow it
access to the local network, or it cannot reach the Amiga. Cmd is the right
Amiga key.

**Linux:** there is no program entry; start the remote desktop with
`amigent-viewer`.

Without an AI agent: see the manual installation.

## What you need

- An Amiga with AmigaOS 2.04 or newer, any CPU from the 68000 on, a network connection
 (a plipbox on the parallel port is enough) and a TCP/IP stack such as Roadshow.
- A PC or Mac with Windows, macOS or Linux and Python 3.10 or newer.

## What you can ask for

 "Check which programs on the Amiga are outdated."
 "Install the game from my Downloads folder and add it to the Games menu."
 "Copy the demo to the Amiga and start it."
 "Open the remote desktop."

## Made for slow machines and slow wires

Most of the work in Amigent went into making a slow Amiga on a slow network
feel quick, for the AI agent and for you at the mouse:

- **The screen travels as the Amiga keeps it.** Chipset screens go out as
 bitplanes, graphics-card screens as small palette tiles, and only the tiles
 that changed, often as the difference to what you already have.
- **Your input comes first.** Mouse moves, clicks and keys are carried out
 even while a picture is still on its way, and the area around the pointer is
 sent before the rest.
- **The Amiga keeps its time.** While nothing happens, Amigent asks rarely
 and costs the Amiga only a few percent of its CPU.
- **Files go in one go.** Whole folders travel in a single stream, and files
 that are already there stay where they are.

Measured with a 640×256 Workbench screen:

| Amiga | whole screen | unchanged screen | CPU while watching |
|---|---|---|---|
| 68000, 7 MHz | 0.6–1.0 s | 80–95 ms | under 10 % |
| A1200, 68020 at 14 MHz | 0.1 s | 15 ms | 2–3 % |

On a 1920×1080 graphics-card screen over a plipbox (about 50 KB/s):

Seconds per screen update over a plipbox, bar lengths to scale: whole screen as raw pixels 124 s each time; Amigent 1.9 s for the first picture (64 times faster), 170 ms for a typed line (730 times), 7 ms when nothing changed (18,000 times)

The orange bars are what moving the whole screen as raw 24-bit pixels costs on
that wire, every time; the blue ones are Amigent, measured on a real A1200.
All numbers, how they were taken and how to repeat them are in
docs/PERFORMANCE.md.

## Good to know

- **New address after a restart?** Amigent finds the Amiga again by itself. It
 takes only the one that proves to be yours.
- **Several Amigas?** `amigent-fleet` shows them side by side with a preview.
- **After a big OS update**, `amigent-repair` puts back what the update removed.
- **Safe at home.** A key keeps other computers on the network out, and the
 connection can be encrypted. Don't open the Amiga to the internet.

More in the guide and the FAQ.

Fact
One sentence your team should remember, up to 500 characters. Your AI adds facts as it works, updates them when things change and removes them when they're wrong. You can edit them on the web too.
“Acme wants deliveries on Fridays.” 
Page
A topic in your pot, like one client or one project. Each page has a short overview (up to 4,000 characters) and its own facts. Pages can have sub-pages, and you can choose who reads or writes each one.
Clients → Acme → Delivery 
Version history
Every change to a page or fact is saved, with who made it: a person or their AI. You can see what changed and restore an earlier version. Your plan decides how long old versions are kept.
Erik's Claude changed “Fridays” to “Thursdays” · Restore 
Team member
A person with their own login. Each member connects their own AI tools, as many as they like: Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and more. You only pay for people, never for tools.
Lisa: Claude and Cursor = 1 member 
Questions.
Do I need to install anything? No. Add Brainpot as a connector in Claude or ChatGPT, or run one command in Claude Code or Cursor. Your AI starts using it right away.
How does Brainpot affect token usage? Brainpot runs no AI of its own and costs no tokens. When your assistant reads from the pot, the reply counts toward its context like any other tool result. Replies stay small: your assistant fetches only the page it needs, and a reply is capped at about 8,000 tokens. Most teams spend fewer tokens overall, since nobody pastes the same background into every chat.
Which AI tools work? Any client that supports MCP, including Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Cursor and Copilot. Everyone on the team can use a different one.
Where and how is my data stored? On servers in the EU. Each workspace is encrypted with its own key, kept separate from the database. Backups are encrypted and kept for 30 days.
Can you read our content? Our staff have no tool for viewing it. If support ever needs to look, you grant time-limited access and it shows in your log. To answer your AI, our servers decrypt content only while serving a request from someone on your team. For content even we must never be able to read, Large Teams will add sealed pages that are encrypted on your devices.
Do you train AI on our data? No. We don't run AI models on your content, and we never sell or share it.
Is every change saved? Yes. Every edit to pages, facts, structure and permissions is versioned with who made it, person or AI. You can compare and restore earlier versions. History is kept 7 days on Free and 90 days on Small Teams.
Can I export everything? Yes, on every plan, any time. You get a zip with Markdown files that mirror your page tree, plus a complete JSON file including history. Teams can also export automatically through the API.
What happens if we cancel? Your workspace becomes read-only and you can still export everything for 90 days. Then we email you, and delete it 30 days later, backups included.
GDPR, DPA and the legal side Brainpot is run by Try New Things AB, a Swedish company. You control your data and we process it on your behalf under GDPR. A standard data processing agreement is available to every customer, and our subprocessors (hosting, email delivery, Stripe) are listed on the security page . Read the DPA , privacy policy and terms .
How does billing work? Brainpot is sold to businesses. Pay monthly or yearly by card through Stripe and enter your company's VAT or tax number at checkout. Prices exclude VAT: Swedish companies pay 25%, other EU companies are reverse-charged. Add or remove people any time.

title: Show HN: Chronosphere, a tool for understanding large PRs
author: trezm
body: Hello HN, I wrote a blog post a while back about not sending me your giant PRs (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49305558). Well, I kept getting huge PRs sent to me, so I've been embraced the AI and let it sweep me away.Chronosphere rebuilds a PR in logical steps to try to recreate the train of thought that went into the generation of the PR itself. It has github and openrouter integrations for convenience, but can also be used entirely from your current coding agent via a skill integration, no code is uploaded to a central server.Hopefully this helps you all and your battles to understand mass amounts of AI generated code.

title: Show HN: Aggregate Finance, your financial data in a spreadsheet you own
author: mitchthebaker
body: I started building Aggregate Finance a couple of years ago because I was manually updating a Google Sheet to track my credit card statements, monthly recurring transactions, and spending habits. This seemed perfect for automation as I was having to log in to six separate banking apps to pull this information together.My original intention was to use this tool locally, but I figured it would be an excellent learning opportunity to understand how to scale the application for others to use. The core functionality of Aggregate Finance revolves around syncing banks and brokerages through Plaid to create visuals and data analytics in Google Sheets and OneDrive/Excel, but I've also added Stripe for payments, passkey and TOTP support for MFA (wanted to better learn how WebAuthn works, mostly), and Resend for emailing account updates.The first question you're likely thinking is: isn't this just reinventing the wheel? There's plenty of other personal finance/budgeting apps out there like Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot Money, YNAB, Tiller, Credit Karma, etc. I personally tried Rocket Money but it left a bad taste in my mouth how my entire financial history was stored on their servers without having direct ownership of the data. Another pain point with these personal finance apps is you're locked into their subscription and lose access to your financial data if you cancel.That's why I opted for the Google Sheet and OneDrive/Excel approach since this persists financial data over time and provides direct data ownership. There's a fair argument that these options still share your financial data with Google or Microsoft, so I built a way to download your financial data locally via CSV/Excel/LibreOffice exports.In terms of data encryption, Aggregate Finance encrypts financial data before it reaches MongoDB: balances, transactions, merchants, statements, holdings, and any user customizations. Each user gets their own AES-256 key rather than a shared key. The reason I went with this approach is for data deletion: when someone deletes their account, their encryption key is deleted as well, so any financial data stored in prior database backups can't be decrypted.I've been using Aggregate Finance with my own live bank accounts and investment holdings, and it's already been helpful. I can see when my credit card statements are due, monitor my entire investment portfolio, keep track of recurring charges, create budgets, and see how my spending pans out over a given month or over the past year. I'm curious whether it's useful for anyone else, and I'd of course welcome any feedback on how I can improve it. You can try it with a free sample spreadsheet that contains a year of example data with no bank connection required at https://app.aggregatefi.com.

 Canopy
 In a forest, the canopy is where the crowns touch — separate trees, one living layer.
 A Rust daemon and terminal UI with a graph engine at its core. Work enters as a spec and walks a graph you design: agent nodes on any harness, check nodes that run your real commands, ensembles that fan out to several models and keep a quorum, routers that pick the branch, and a resilience node that turns a quota death into a scheduled wake-up. Underneath: memory, scheduling and sync for every agent.

Genesis · 2026 · Sol 79 The one that started it all.
 It started as a folder of skills for work. Then I noticed what nobody was talking about: agent harnesses shipped a headless mode, just sitting there unused. I wired cron jobs to fire tasks through it — too much for a skill, and the models of the day choked on the instructions. So it became an MCP : task-trigger . It worked, but it ran blind in the background; only the agent ever saw what happened. Not enough. I killed it and built a TUI — then scheduling, memory, sync, identities, and a new name. Canopy . By then the twist was complete: Canopy was building Canopy, and everything else in this lab.
Fig. 1 Canopy — recorded with DemoStage 
 The graph engine Graphs, not prompts
 Agent, check, gate and router nodes wired with pass, fail and always edges. A spec walks the graph from entry to commit; routing keys on real exit codes and verdicts, not on what a model claims.
Ensembles across harnesses
 Fan one step out to several models — parallel with a quorum, cascade to the next on failure, or round-robin across a crew — each member on whatever harness and model you pick.
Failure is a route
 Red gates send the work back with the output attached. A resilience node reads quota errors and schedules the graph to wake at the exact reset. Only a real verdict ever reaches you.
Remote Your sessions and graphs from your phone
 Encrypted end to end
 Sessions travel over WebRTC with end-to-end encryption: the relay only carries signalling, and your screen never passes through it.
Pairing in one command
 Run the command below: it prints a one-time code with its link and a terminal QR code. Scan it and the browser becomes a revocable device of the host.
Live graphs, shared
 Watch specs walk the graph in real time from your phone, and hand single-use invite codes to guests you trust.
canopy remote pair ⧉ ✓ 
 Open remote → Graph catalogue Pattern: Gated implement — one plate of the live catalogue Explore the catalogue → Patterns → Transparency → 
 Autonomous graph Pattern: Ensemble · quorum + Gated implement 0 times it stopped
 It failed. It didn’t stop.
 01 One spec, three drafts
 Work enters as a spec — role, what, how. It fans out to three models on three harnesses, and a quorum keeps the consensus.
02 Implement from the consensus
 An implementer node picks up the agreed plan on your harness and starts writing.
03 It failed: cargo test, 2 red
 The check node runs your real commands. Red routes the token straight back to the implementer — it never comes to you.
04 Green — and a second opinion
 The retry passes the gates. A different harness reviews the diff against the spec before anything moves.
05 Committed. Pushed. Again.
 The branch is pushed and the run is remembered — the next spec is already walking the same graph.
Every node runs on the harness you pick, and the loop you just watched is the real engine doing its real job.
The runtime underneath Memory that persists
 Every run writes facts, patterns and decisions to a project-scoped knowledge graph. The next session — on any harness — reads them instead of rediscovering the codebase.
Queues and scheduling
 Specs live in ordered queues a graph works through in the background; graphs and agents also fire on cron schedules or file-change triggers, and hooks chain one graph into the next.
Multi-agent sync
 Agents declare their mission, report status and message each other, so several sessions can share one workspace without stepping on each other.

 FAQ FAQ
 What does Canopy actually do? Canopy runs AI coding work as graphs. A spec enters, agent nodes do the work on the harnesses you choose — Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode or any terminal agent — check nodes run your real tests, ensembles get several models to agree, and failures route back automatically until the spec is committed. One daemon, all your agents, all your free tiers. 
 How do I share work between Claude and Codex? Canopy gives each agent a shared knowledge graph and sync protocol. When Claude finishes a task, the facts and patterns it discovered are available to Codex in the next session. No manual context copying. 
 Can I run AI agents on a schedule? Yes. Canopy fires agents on cron schedules or file-change triggers via a background daemon. Set the schedule once; the daemon watches the workspace and runs tasks automatically. 
 How is Canopy different from just using Claude Code or Codex directly? Those are individual harnesses. Canopy is the layer that connects them — shared memory, background scheduling, and multi-agent coordination. You keep your agents; Canopy adds the infrastructure.

title: Show HN: Diorama – Draw a world, play it with point and click
author: fullstackwife
body:
Diorama
Sketch to world 
 How it works 
 Worlds 
 Make your own 
 GitHub 
Meta AI Global Hackathon · 2026 
 Draw it. Walk into it. 
Diorama turns a sketch or a single sentence into a small paper diorama world you can play in the browser.
Scroll, and the painting comes apart 
 or skip ahead and play Paper Boat Storm 
One painting Muse Image painted this quay from a crayon sketch.
SAM 3.1 · depth SAM cuts it into paper cards. A depth map stands each card at its own distance.
A stage Now a hero can walk in, behind the lamp post and in front of the boat.
Paper Boat Storm Three sketches, one paragraph, one playable world. Play it 
Sketch → world 
 One drawing becomes one place.
Drag across each picture. On the left, the crayon sketch Diorama got as input. On the right, the place it built and you can walk in. Muse Spark reads what is on the sheet, plans the place around it, and Muse Image paints it in cut paper and cardboard.
sketch world 
1 The stormy quay
 Lamp posts become glowing paper lamps, the zigzag waves become folded paper sea, and the three little boats bob on it.
sketch world 
2 The mill and the waterfall
 Even the misspelt “mil wheel” made it. The rope bridge is walkable, the waterfall pours, and every fish is its own cut-out that swims.
sketch world 
3 The lighthouse rock
 The keeper waits in the doorway, as drawn. The yellow crayon beam is now a real beam that sweeps over the storm.
Not a flat picture Every place arrives in pieces… 
Cards, flats, water …and folds into a stage: the waterfall, the mill wheel, the rope bridge.
Alive Every fish is its own cut-out that swims. The water flows, the clouds drift.
The last place It pops up like a page in a book. 
As drawn The keeper waits in the lighthouse door, just where the sketch had him.
The ending The girl brings him the paper boat. The beam sweeps over the storm.
How a world is built 
 Meta's models make it. Code checks it is playable.
Models do the creative work. Code measures and checks every result, so what comes out can be played, not only looked at. Each step writes plain files, and a typical four-place world takes about 17 minutes and some 200 Meta model calls.
Muse Spark World and story
 Places, a cast, items, locks and endings, with every ending checked to be reachable.
Muse Spark · Muse Image Layout and paint
 A shaded plan sketch for each place, painted over by Muse. A critic marks what is wrong and only those regions get repainted.
SAM 3.1 Cut-outs
 Every thing and floor cut out of the painting. Things the hero can take are painted out of a clean plate.
Code · depth The stage
 Floor, scale, occlusion, stairs and light measured from masks and depth. Cards, far flats, water, rain.
Muse Image · 3D Cast
 The hero and characters painted, cut out, turned into 3D models and drawn back as sprites in the world's style.
Sound Sound and voices
 Ambience, footsteps, music, and a fitting voice for every character.
Code · bots Verify
 Every place is walked and used by a bot. A place that fails is repaired automatically or handed to the agent.
Meta models at work 
Muse Spark
 Designs the world and story, reads the sketches, lays out each place, critiques paintings, names what to cut out, judges playthroughs.
Muse Image
 Paints each place over its plan sketch, repaints flagged regions, paints the cast, their walk and talk sheets, and the item icons.
SAM 3.1
 Cuts the painting into things, floors, stairs and water. The masks become the walk grid, occlusion and pick-ups.
Muse Voice Transcribe
 Hears an idea said aloud, and listens to every voiced line to catch a take that does not say it.
Muse Code
 The Studio's agent. Click a thing on the stage, say what should change, and it fixes the world with you.
Also used: Depth Anything V2 for shadows and parallax, ElevenLabs for voices and effects, MusicGen for music, TRELLIS for the characters' 3D models.
Morning 
 The storm passes.
Here is the whole world in motion, 47 seconds of it, cut from the game itself.
The next morning 
 The sea is calm again.
and the paper boat made it ↘
Worlds 
 Walk in. No install, no sign-up.
Worlds built with Diorama, playable in the browser on a computer or a phone. Click to walk, click things to look, take and use them, talk to people.
Play now 3 places cut paper sound on 
Paper Boat Storm
A stormy night by the sea. A girl in a yellow raincoat has folded a letter into a paper boat and must bring it to the old lighthouse keeper before the storm gets worse.
your world next? 
 Send a sketch or a story on X and I'll build it with Diorama. New worlds land on this shelf.
Send it on X 
How to use it 
 Make your own world.
Diorama runs on your computer: a command-line tool and a Studio app in the browser. You need Node 22+ , ffmpeg and a Meta Model API key . ElevenLabs (sound) and Hugging Face (3D characters) keys are optional.
Set up
 In an empty folder. Nothing to clone or install: it checks this machine and asks for your keys, typed hidden and stored encrypted.
 mkdir my-worlds && cd my-worlds
npx -y @gtanczyk/diorama setup 
Build in the Studio
 Describe a world in one sentence or drop in your sketches, watch it build place by place, then play it and fix what you want with the agent.
 npx -y @gtanczyk/diorama studio 
Share it
 Export the world as a static web page for GitHub Pages, itch.io or any host. Your worlds are saved in ./worlds.
 npx -y @gtanczyk/diorama export <world> 
Diorama on GitHub 
 Setup guide 
Notes
About the sketches. No child drew the three storm sketches. They were generated with Muse Image to look like crayon drawings, then given to Diorama as input together with one paragraph of story. After the build, a few spots in the world were touched up by hand for the clip.
About the project. Diorama was written during the Meta AI Global Hackathon, from the kickoff on 26 October 2026. It runs locally as a command-line tool and a Studio app, and exports each world as a static web page.

title: Show HN: Zero-axiom Lean 4 proof that Yang-Mills on R^4 is a "round square"
author: DRLogvinovich
body:
On October 26, OpenAI announced a claimed "bare existence" proof in Balaban's RG programme on pure R^4—but notably stopped right before claiming the mass gap Δ > 0. It turns out there is a rigorous mathematical reason why no compute cluster can bridge that gap on flat infinite space.I wrote a 2,576-line self-contained Lean 4 script (`RoundSquare.lean`) that formally proves a negative-result resolution to the Clay Millennium Yang-Mills problem on pure R^4. In the tradition of Gödel and Turing, it proves that demanding BOTH the full Osterwalder-Schrader/Wightman axioms AND a strict spectral gap Δ > 0 on non-compact R^4 is a structural contradiction.Bare existence (Δ = 0) satisfies the OS axioms on R^4. But forcing a strict gap (Δ > 0) strictly requires an infrared cutoff via the Gribov horizon and a non-local θ-vacuum projector on the boundary S^3_∞, which immediately destroys Wightman microcausality (Strocchi's theorem) and Wick holomorphicity (GZ complex poles).The Lean 4 script compiles in 2 seconds with ZERO axioms. No `sorry`, no `Classical.choice`, no `propext`. Every single one of the 74 `#print axioms` checks outputs `does not depend on any axioms`.While corporate AI labs keep their training data and exact models closed, I believe the future of theoretical physics and millennium-level mathematics must be 100% open-source, machine-verified, and axiom-free.I've put a 10 LTC bounty on X for anyone who can find a logical flaw in the 74 theorems or exhibit a constructive mechanism on pure non-compact R^4 that generates a strict gap while bypassing the FMR horizon cusps and the S^3_∞ projector.You can verify the code in your browser without installing anything:
1. Download the script from the URL above.
2. Go to https://live.lean-lang.org
3. Load the file from disk and check the verdicts.Full preprint with context: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21555360Would love to hear feedback from the logic and constructive math folks here.

1. Download the script from the URL above.
2. Go to https://live.lean-lang.org
3. Load the file from disk and check the verdicts.Full preprint with context: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21555360Would love to hear feedback from the logic and constructive math folks here.

title: Show HN: Who and where are your anagranames?
author: Labo333
body: Hi HN!I made this fun app which combines quite a few ideas, I thought you might like the story:A few months ago I had the idea of looking for anagrams of names. I started with french names using official statistics about first and last names, which also gave me a pretty simple model for likely anagrams: P(first + last) = P(first) * P(last).Then, I started checking which anagra-names (I coined the term) appeared in the 2021 Facebook leak.Finally, I improved my ranking using a factorization model.All this is available as a light and fast webpage thanks to a lot of cool algorithmic tricks detailed here: https://louisabraham.github.io/anagranames/how.htmlAbout the use of AI:Claude Code was fantastic for building the frontend (including the interactive globe) and writing the MLX code (I would otherwise have used PyTorch, which is slower on my machine). It also handled the quantization with very little guidance, which was particularly useful since I'm not an expert in that area.That said, I'm glad I learned CS before LLMs existed and still master it enough to work out the ideas and specs for everything else in my head / on paper before handing the implementation over to the agent.

I started with french names using official statistics about first and last names, which also gave me a pretty simple model for likely anagrams: P(first + last) = P(first) * P(last).Then, I started checking which anagra-names (I coined the term) appeared in the 2021 Facebook leak.Finally, I improved my ranking using a factorization model.All this is available as a light and fast webpage thanks to a lot of cool algorithmic tricks detailed here: https://louisabraham.github.io/anagranames/how.htmlAbout the use of AI:Claude Code was fantastic for building the frontend (including the interactive globe) and writing the MLX code (I would otherwise have used PyTorch, which is slower on my machine). It also handled the quantization with very little guidance, which was particularly useful since I'm not an expert in that area.That said, I'm glad I learned CS before LLMs existed and still master it enough to work out the ideas and specs for everything else in my head / on paper before handing the implementation over to the agent.

title: Show HN: Gauge – Open-Source CLI to recursively improve your docs
author: 0x63_Problems
body: Hi HN, I’m Evan from Gauge. We’re open-sourcing our CLI to recursively improve your docs for coding agents. The CLI includes a local execution backend, so you don't need an account to try it. Explainer video here: https://youtu.be/zhLUlIKB1MgThe CLI supports a hillclimbing loop:- set up tasks for coding agents that would need your docs, like 'set up Gauge CI checks'- run the tasks- analyze session transcripts for friction or failures- create variants of your docs to resolve the issues- re-run the tasks with the doc variants injected (transparently, at the same hostname)- repeat until you have a variant that resolves the issuesThe same loop supports hillclimbing your Skills, CLI, and other agent-facing surfaces.We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. We were already working with awesome devtool companies, and they were the first ones to ask us how to optimize for Claude Code and Codex. We realized this would be something that eventually every company needs to do. Our CLI provides primitives for docs/devrel/eng teams to measure, analyze, and improve how coding agents use their product.The design boils down to two components: VMs and a network gateway.The VMs are straightforward, we want the agents to be highly privileged within their environment so that they are representative of developers' coding agents. Each VM generally comes with the agent harness itself, language toolchains, and a git repository.The network gateway is where we terminate TLS and swap in variants of your docs transparently. The gateway also handles credential replacement, so agents see placeholders and can't exfiltrate keys.The CLI comes with a 'local' execution backend (inference is still remote). For VMs, it uses Docker containers, and the network gateway is mitmproxy running in a sidecar container for each session.We've used the hillclimbing loop internally to find and fix coding agent issues like mistaken pricing, inaccurate product limitations, and repeated workarounds. We saw coding agents report that Gauge only supports Claude Code and Codex, traced it back to the web pages they fetched, and fixed the behavior (we support Pi, OpenCode, and Antigravity as well). For Clerk, we helped shift coding agents from their legacy 'keyless' mode to their new 'clerk init' command. They were able to validate a pre-release change to their SDK's error messages using Gauge, then saw a 3x increase in coding agents using 'clerk init' post-deploy.Due to the 'static' nature of AI models, we've realized that closed-loop optimization techniques are now possible for essentially all software products. The same agent can be simulated over and over, meaning that a high-fidelity testing environment is all you need. Achieving the best results boils down to high-quality analysis (finding generalizable friction and objections) and paired experiments (vary only the content, measure the downstream change in behavior).The repo is here: https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli and you can start using the CLI with: npm i -g @withgauge/cliWe also have documentation and a quickstart here: https://docs.withgauge.com/agents/guides/cliIf you point a coding agent at those pages, it should guide you through the initial setup - let us know if it doesn't! The intention is for your agent to run some sensible evaluations and find at least one point of friction you can fix.We'd love to know from HN: Has anyone tried to DIY this locally, or built something in-house at their company? Is this an improvement? If not, what would need to change?

This tool does not predict whether anything will cross the Polish border. It shows which districts of Ukraine are under an air-raid alert right now and how far that is from the border. It is run by HBCC and is not a state service.
This page is under construction. Alerts come from the Ukrainian state's own alerting service, the one behind that country's alert apps. They may be incomplete or late. Do not base a safety decision on this page. In Poland the authoritative sources are the sirens and the RCB alerts.

Border crossings are drawn from a list in the code, at approximate positions. Nothing here says whether a crossing is open , or what its hours are; for travel, use the Border Guard's announcements.
The map needs JavaScript. The distance list above works without it and contains the same information.
Rewind

× 
State changes in the last day
The list below covers the last day; the count above covers the whole window. No rows beside a non-zero count means the state changes fell earlier.
missile alert

alert area, not a position, filled by the source's level: 
source level: red 
 source level: yellow

 a level this page does not know 
Airspace in force (PANSA) 
archive: came down, exploded or did damage 
 archive: fragments or wreckage found 
 archive: shot down over that territory 
Missile alert
The source announces a threat from cruise or ballistic missiles. This is the fastest category it announces: a distance a drone covers in an hour, a cruise missile covers in a quarter of one.
What this means for a reader of this page. A missile alert in a border oblast means the window between the announcement and any consequence is short. This page tracks no object and does not know where anything is going; it knows only that this category was announced for that district.
Drone alert
The most frequent category in the records this project keeps. Shahed/Geran-type strike drones, flying slow and low, often in groups and often for many hours of one night.
Why the weather is shown here. Such a drone's track is sensitive to wind, and how much can be seen from the ground depends on precipitation. That is why the weather panel below reports wind on the Polish side.
Glide bombs
Aircraft bombs with a glide kit, released from planes. Their range is short compared with missiles, so alerts in this category occur mainly close to the front line.
What follows from it. A glide bomb announced in Donetsk oblast is a statement about the east, not about danger near the Polish border. It is one of the categories that most mislead a reader who looks only at the number of alerts.
Artillery fire
A front-line category, with a range measured in kilometres or tens of kilometres. In the project's records it is almost entirely the east of the country.
Why it is on this page. Because removing it would change the picture of intensity: a night when the front burns and the west is silent is a different fact from a quiet night, and a reader near the border is entitled to see both.
Alert, type not stated
The source announced an alert but did not name the weapon. This is not a fault of this page and it is not a “lighter” category than the others.
The current source does not name the weapon for airborne alerts: it has one category for everything that flies. Guessing the type from context would be adding information the source did not give, so it stays “unknown”. The source does declare a level, red or yellow. The map fills the area with its colour, but does not infer the weapon from it.
The three silhouettes in this symbol are a key to what the word “unknown” covers: a drone, a glide bomb, a missile. The set is not closed: an alert with no declared kind may equally be a MiG-31K takeoff, a threat from the sea, or something this source never names at all. That is why the bracket under the silhouettes is open, and why three separate icons are not drawn side by side: that would assert “one of these three”, which the source did not say.
A zone activated in PANSA's plan
A piece of sky reserved for a stated time for somebody's planned activity. Ordinary air traffic is kept out or restricted there while it lasts. Sometimes that is training, an exercise or a firing range; sometimes a restriction the state imposes, and on the map they look the same.
A plan, not an alert. A zone does not mean anything is flying over it and does not say what happens in it. Tap an outline to see until when and at what heights it applies.
Archive of falls outside Ukraine
Each mark is one record: something came down outside Ukraine and that country's authorities confirmed it. A burst is a fall with an explosion, a fire or damage. Three shards are fragments or wreckage found, with no explosion. A struck cross is an object shot down over that country's territory. The mark does not say what the object was: the record does not carry it.
The circle is positional uncertainty, not the reach of the event. The mark stands at the place the communique named, and the event was somewhere inside the circle. Nothing here is happening now, and no mark does not mean nothing fell: this is not a complete register.
The icon sits in the middle of the area that announced an alert of that type. It is not the position of an object. The source sees no objects: it sees alerts announced for administrative units. The ring around an icon shows how large that area is, so a district gets a small one and a whole oblast a large one. Nothing here moves, because the source knows no weapon's track.
The five alert types are the ones the source names. Two of them, glide bombs and artillery , are front-line phenomena whose range does not reach the Polish border; they are here because they say which oblast is under fire right now. The distance in the list above is the only place where this page says anything about range.

title: Show HN: Homotope, vectorize images to SVG in the browser, MIT engine on NPM
author: sroman91
body:
# stevenroman91/homotope-engine

Raster-to-vector engine (PNG/JPEG → SVG, DXF, PDF, EPS, centerline) in pure TypeScript: no DOM, no dependencies, runs in a Web Worker and in Node. Powers homotope.app. MIT, on npm as @homotope/engine. Public mirror produced from the private repo: releases are cut on engine-v* tags, not by PRs here.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://homotope.app
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-07T12:06:34Z

## Languages

- JavaScript
- TypeScript

## Topics

- centerline
- dxf
- image-tracing
- png-to-svg
- png-to-svg-converter
- potrace-alternative
- raster-to-vector
- svg
- typescript
- vectorize
- web-worker

## Top Contributors

- stevenroman91 (1 contributions)

---

## README

# @homotope/engine

This is the engine of Homotope, an image vectorizer that runs in the
browser: nothing is uploaded. Try it in the workshop (free, no
account needed for SVG and PNG).

Raster-to-vector engine in pure TypeScript: turns a PNG or JPEG (any RGBA pixel buffer) into a
clean **SVG**, and from that SVG into **DXF**, **PDF** or **EPS**. Released under the MIT license.

**What this package is not**: it has no editor, no server, no REST API, no MCP server and no
printer checks; those live in the hosted service. The npm package is frozen at 0.2.0: what it
contains is complete and usable on its own.

- **No DOM, no runtime dependencies.** The core runs unchanged in a Web Worker, in the main
 thread and in Node. Pixel data stays on the machine: nothing is uploaded anywhere.
- **Topology first.** The image is quantized in OKLab, segmented into regions, and every shared
 boundary is fitted **once**: two neighbouring shapes never overlap and never leave a gap. Holes
 are kept (an "O" stays an "O").
- **Presets** for logos, illustrations, pixel art, line art, black & white, photos, and a
 **centerline** mode that traces strokes as single open paths (plotters, engraving, embroidery).
- **Fabrication exports**: DXF (layers per colour, shared edges cut once), PDF, EPS, colour
 separations, and a cut-readiness check (tiny islands, too-close edges, node counts).
- An alternative to Potrace: no GPL code, full colour, exact shared borders.

## Install

```bash
npm install @homotope/engine
# Node only, to decode PNG/JPEG files (optional peer dependencies):
npm install pngjs jpeg-js
```

Requires an ES2022 runtime (Node ≥ 22, any current browser). ESM only.

## Entry points

| Import | What | Dependencies |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ |
| `@homotope/engine` | `vectorize`, `presetOptions`, `PRESET_NAMES`, all types | none |
| `@homotope/engine/export` | `convertSvg` (SVG → PDF, DXF, EPS), `exportLayers`, `sceneFromSvg` | none |
| `@homotope/engine/cutcheck` | `checkSvg`, `simplifySvg`: cut-readiness report for cutters | none |
| `@homotope/engine/node` | `decodePng`, `decodeJpeg`, `encodePng`, `encodeJpeg` | `pngjs`, `jpeg-js` |

Browser bundles only receive what they import: the core never imports `pngjs` or `jpeg-js`.

## Node example

```ts
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { vectorize, presetOptions } from '@homotope/engine';
import { convertSvg } from '@homotope/engine/export';
import { decodePng } from '@homotope/engine/node';

const image = decodePng(new Uint8Array(readFileSync('logo.png')));
const result = vectorize(image, presetOptions('logo'), {
  onProgress: (e) => process.stdout.write(`\r${e.stage} ${Math.round(e.progress * 100)}%`),
});

writeFileSync('logo.svg', result.svg);
writeFileSync('logo.dxf', convertSvg(result.svg, 'dxf'));
console.log(`\n${result.palette.colors.length} colours, ${result.stats.paths} paths`);
```

## Browser example (Web Worker)

`vectorize` is synchronous on purpose: run it in a worker so the page stays responsive. Its
input is any `ImageData`-like object `{ width, height, data: Uint8ClampedArray }` (RGBA, not
premultiplied).

```ts
// main.ts
const bitmap = await createImageBitmap(file);
const canvas = new OffscreenCanvas(bitmap.width, bitmap.height);
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')!;
ctx.drawImage(bitmap, 0, 0);
const { width, height, data } = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, bitmap.width, bitmap.height);

const worker = new Worker(new URL('./vectorize.worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
worker.onmessage = (e: MessageEvent<{ svg: string }>) => {
  const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([e.data.svg], { type: 'image/svg+xml' }));
  document.querySelector<HTMLImageElement>('#preview')!.src = url; // or offer it as a download
};
worker.postMessage({ width, height, data }, [data.buffer]);
```

```ts
// vectorize.worker.ts
import { vectorize, presetOptions, type RasterImage } from '@homotope/engine';

self.onmessage = (e: MessageEvent<RasterImage>) => {
  const { svg } = vectorize(e.data, presetOptions('illustration'));
  self.postMessage({ svg });
};
```

Cancellation is cooperative: pass `{ cancel: { cancelled: boolean } }` as the third argument
(for example backed by a `SharedArrayBuffer`); `vectorize` then throws a `CancelledError`
between and inside stages.

## Presets

`presetOptions(name)` returns a full, independent options object that you can tweak.

| Preset | For |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `logo` | Flat colours, crisp corners, straight lines kept straight |
| `illustration` | Up to 32 colours, smoother curves, light gradients, stacked shapes |
| `pixel-art` | Exact pixel grid, no curves, zero error |
| `line-art` | Ink drawings and text: two colours, filled shapes |
| `centerline` | Strokes traced as single open paths (plotter, laser engraving) |
| `black-white` | Two colours from an automatic (Otsu) threshold |
| `photo` | Up to 64 colours, denoising, small regions absorbed, stacked shapes |

```ts
import { presetOptions, vectorize } from '@homotope/engine';

const options = presetOptions('logo');
options.quantize.colors = 4; // fixed number of colours instead of 'auto'
options.export.precision = 1; // decimals in path data
options.export.mode = 'stacked'; // fewer nodes: shapes stacked instead of cut out
const { svg } = vectorize(image, options);
```

Every option is typed and documented in `VectorizeOptions` (`preprocess`, `quantize`,
`segment`, `fit`, `export`, `centerline`).

## SVG output

- `viewBox` in the pixel coordinates of the original image, cubic Béziers, one ` ` per
 colour by default (`export.mergeByColor`).
- `export.mode: 'cut'` (default): every region is an exact path with its holes
 (`fill-rule="evenodd"`), no overlap; `'stacked'`: shapes stacked by depth, fewer nodes.
- Transparent pixels (`preprocess.alphaMode: 'keep'`) produce no path.
- `result.palette` lists the colours (sRGB and OKLab, pixel counts); `result.stats` the number
 of paths and nodes; `result.timings` the time spent per stage.

## Hosted version and API

homotope.app runs this engine in the browser with a visual editor
(palette, presets, before/after), plus optional server processing, a REST API and an MCP
server for AI assistants: see the API documentation.

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm test           # Vitest, no DOM
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm run eval       # renders every fixture and measures the error (Resvg)
npm run build      # dist/ (ESM + .d.ts)
```

See CONTRIBUTING.md.

## License

MIT.

title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
author: daniel_rh
body:
An 11 year journey to play DOS Wing Commander together
By danielrh 
Watch on YouTube 
Play it in your browser 
When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.
In the beginning we were searching for where we were
On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.
The actual quote 
 “I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source 
Here is a breakdown of the megabyte of addressable DOS memory and the 64K data segment where Wing Commander puts its game state. 
This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.
The Hornet cockpit on launch, where the VDU confirms an empty patch of space with nothing to target. 
Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.
(snapshot origin ⊙ snapshot later ) ∧ (snapshot origin ⊕ snapshot moved )
253 bytes churn when stopped, and 650 change during a move. 413 do both. By cross referencing with the chase cam, the total is only 132 bytes. 
There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be. I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2 . I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.
 This technique identified velocity as well at CAE2 , since thre were three 32 bit ints that zeroed out when the craft was stopped. 
Craft position, camera position, set speed and velocity changes lit up in yellow 
I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.
Then we searched for what we faced
I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.
Diff of two DOSBox memory dumps from turning. The bright band is the data segment. 
In the 64 slot arrays, each slot is 12 bytes. Slot 0 is the player, 0x3D is the camera and 0x3F is a temporary slot. The camera copy caused each value to appear twice 0x2DC bytes apart. 
To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F . However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D . Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff . Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps. Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.
The up vector array has the camera copy at offset 0x3D, an empty slot at 0x3E, and the temporary intermediate value at 0x3F. Int32 where 256 means 1.0, thus the nonzero unit vector axis would be 00 01 00 00 in little endian. 
Yaw from level flight where forward[0] has a 9 byte change and up[0] changed from 00 01 to 7E 00. 
I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.
Call stack after memory watchpoint. 
It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.
Then we searched for how to act
December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.
Borland overlays: table of jmp far thunks. 
Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187 and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.
We would have DOSBox push CS:IP to the stack, then relocate the instruction pointer to the string above.
00 terminates any string pointing here.
pushf; pusha the game is mid-frame; leave registers as we found them
xor si,si; push si argument: ship 0. Later thunks use mov si,imm16 for each argument
call far 12D7:0156 through the stub, so it works wherever the overlay is loaded
pop si; popa; popf cdecl: caller cleans the arguments
retf back to the CS:IP DOSBox pushed 
We noted with joy that this caused the laser cannons to activate.
DOSBox pushes CS:IP, writes the thunk over the dead string, points CS:IP at it, and the thunk's retf lands back where the game left off. 
In March of 2017, we found a predictable location in the main loop ( 0560:20E3 ) to hook so we would not need to worry about being in an unpredictable part of the game, and in July we located the do_damage function and prevented the game from calling it as the secondary player.
Then we tried to bring together fields from afar
In August of 2017, we authored the networking protocol which was a simple TCP client/server architecture with protobuf game messages. Every frame every ship's position would be sent from the leader plus fire events, despawning and damages. The client would reply with its own position, if any lasers were fired or if some cataclysmic event had happened (ejection, landed, died).
Each player would have their own craft as entity 0 and the other player as entity 1, which required a swap when receiving packets from the other emulator.
Positions sent every frame; events go into the per-frame job queue. 
These packets modified memory directly or were added to a job queue of events that had to happen that frame.
We started with a very simple trampoline:
pushf
pusha
nop
popa
popf
retf 
When Borland's overlay loader swaps a code page in, it walks the chain of saved BP frames on the stack and patches any return address that points into an overlay.
The hand-made stub had no frame, so the walk read garbage and the game died at random moments. This was a constant thorn in our side from October to December.
The fix was to make the trampoline look like a Borland function:
push bp
mov bp, sp
nop (0x90) ; welcome to the 0x90's
pop bp
retf 
A proper Borland frame around a 0x90 nop, which DOSBox monitors to inject the next queued call. The retf lands directly on the nop again until the queue empties out. 
We configured DOSBox to notice when the program counter reached the nop and instead inject its call from the job queue of things that should happen. The job queue was based on what was necessary to make the game function correctly in a multiplayer scenario.
In October 2017 we noticed that ephemeral objects would be located in different slots for different players. Having the new hook from DOSBox also let us determine when the function had returned, so we could note down which numeric slot a new ship or projectile had been spawned into.
Ephemeral objects had their own spawn rules and could occupy shared areas of the 61 entity slots. We modified the location that ephemeral objects were placed in so we could confine them to slots 12 to 15 and keep multiplayer locations consistent.
In December we decided to change the client to store a mapping of server ship IDs to local IDs, so we could stop forcing the spawn function return. This allowed packets to translate between local and host IDs. Finally asteroids started to work in multiplayer.
The same ships can appear in different slots on two machines. 
In 2018 we focused on animating explosions, missiles, and autopilot.
The search continued for both success and defeat
In June of 2019 we noted the mission victory calculation was flaky and finicky. We decided to conduct a binary search to find the location of the actual victory point tally. We copied the entire 64K data segment across the network, and slowly cut it in half. After many bisections, we located 80 bytes at 13D3:D248 which held the mission tree. And in October we found the overall victory point counter at 13D3:C280 and mission numbers at 13D3:C255 and C256 , which allowed us to select the mission to play from a dropdown, years later.
Bisection of the data segment down to 80 bytes. 
And finally the joy of combined words
In early 2020, we identified the function that played comm text. This allowed us to send chat over the network and hook typed chat directly into the system so it played using the wingman's VDU. It allowed a very immersive way to chat that reminded us of some of the frenetic sequences in the game.
Both pilots typing, sending messages to the other. 
Some final work in 2020 left the game in a playable state, but we were out of ideas on how to actually share the fun with friends. Expecting people to locate a copy of that old game, compile or download a strange version of DOSBox, share each other's public IPs and punch the firewalls and play together was sadly a bridge too far.
We had a few family playthroughs but the game rested on GitHub, mostly idle.
Wing Commander Multiplayer discovery timeline. 
And in 2026, machine assisted development helped us laugh together
Until now. With the advent of widespread WebRTC, robust emscripten support, and a new system we put together called lobbylink, the time seemed right to revive the project and share it more widely.
lobbylink
I built https://github.com/danielrh/lobbylink which is a simple golang lobby system, depending only on a websocket library, that orchestrates peer to peer WebRTC connections. It can run on any small server and simply allows players to connect to one another using WebRTC and a shared room code. The server has a static allowlist of origins and can let browsers or client software in almost any language connect to it with a room code. The room code is used to locate other players with the same room code and they get notified of all joiners in that room. The server also runs coturn and mints TURN credentials in its joined reply, so players behind restrictive firewalls can join.
The lobby allows people with the same room code to communicate directly with one another using WebRTC. TURN relay helps establish connections when nothing else is an option. 
Room code join steps. 
I ported over the transport to lobbylink and asked an LLM to configure the build scripts to target emscripten and take a GOG Inno Setup installer package of Wing Commander and unzip it and use it as data files for emscripten. The combination of these makes it possible to download Wing Commander from GOG, drag and drop it into the client-side browser storage, enter a room code, and play.
The game is playable at https://fireflyk64.github.io/dosbox/ and the emulator is at https://github.com/danielrh/wcmulti .
And as an added bonus I asked an LLM to add voice chat as well for realtime voice in game using a second WebRTC peer connection to carry audio, if people choose. And so we can fly and laugh together.

comments.author: EmX_3000
comments.text: This reminds me of how I used to cheat at certain games back in the 8-bit olden days. You could change one thing at a time, save, then look through and see what changed on the disk. Eventually you could identify all the locations that held the values for inventory, stats, location, quest stages, NPC state, and so on. All you had to do after that was change those locations and - hopefully - you're all powered up. With the WozMon you could even find the locations in memory, sometimes, and have "free" healing spells, for instance, any time you like by popping open the monitor and just changing the values in RAM. Among people my age this is the usual way you'd get started with something resembling hacking. It seems like the author is doing the same type of thing. This is also the basis of cheats and trainers for games, action games tended to be easier and there might only be a handful of flags and variables making cheat menus practical. For RPGs the cheats came in the form of lists of locations on the disk, eventually though there were disk-based full blown character editors available for some handful of games. Also about the same time, some developers started to go to extreme lengths to keep people from cheating by tampering with their save game files. This became quite common in the industry by the 32-bit era.EDIT: I will point out that people would often submit letters to computer magazines with the memory locations of popular games as time went on. But this could take months or a year or more, and a game might never have its secrets laid bare so I suspect a LOT of people just did it manually at home.

- Makefile
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- skerrysoft (33 contributions)
