## README

# safeagent

**A lightweight Linux VM for every checkout, so parallel coding sessions
can't collide, and the code they run can't reach your machine.**

Coding agents like Claude Code work best in parallel: several sessions, each
in its own git worktree, each on its own task. Worktrees separate the files,
but everything else is shared. Two sessions both want port 3000, one
branch's migration breaks the other's database, and every command an agent
runs has your whole machine within reach.

safeagent gives each worktree its own small Linux VM, with its own processes,
ports, Postgres, Valkey (Redis) and Temporal, and its own copy of their data.
It reads what it needs from the repository (lockfiles, compose files,
monorepo packages, the local addresses its env files name), so most
projects need no configuration. It plugs
into Claude Code, so every worktree session gets one automatically and the
VM is ready in the background while the session gets on with the work; with
any other tool, `safeagent create` makes a workspace by hand.

Two live Claude Code sessions side by side, each in its own safeagent workspace. As they start, the status line shows safeagent preparing each workspace in the background (building the VM image) while Claude reads and edits code. One adds a --quantity option and places an order for two espresso machines; the other merges a branch that brings a new migration and places an order for a teapot with the gift note "Happy birthday!". Each workspace has its own Postgres and Temporal, so both orders are order #1.

*Two real Claude Code sessions, recorded live with
asciinema (idle time trimmed to 2 s; nothing else
edited). As each session opens, safeagent prepares its workspace in the
background (the VM, Postgres, Temporal, `npm install`, migrations), shown
in the status line, while Claude gets on with the code. Each has its own
database: both place order #1, and only the second, which merged a branch
with a new migration, has a `gift_note` column.*

> **Status: early development.** macOS on Apple Silicon today; Linux hosts
> are being built. See What works today.

---

## Get started with Claude Code

**1. Install safeagent** on a Mac with Apple Silicon:

```bash
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent/releases/latest/download/safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && tar -xzf safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz -C ~/.local/bin   # or anywhere on your PATH
```

Each release is built by GitHub Actions
from this repository, with checksums (`SHA256SUMS`) and a signed build
provenance attestation. To check a download was built here, before
installing it:

```bash
gh attestation verify safeagent-darwin-arm64.tar.gz --repo skerrysoft/safeagent
```

Downloaded it with a browser instead? macOS then won't run it ("cannot be
opened"), as it isn't notarized yet; clear the download flag with
`xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/safeagent`.

 
 Or build it from source (Go 1.27+) 

```bash
git clone https://github.com/skerrysoft/safeagent && cd safeagent
make build                      # bin/safeagent, signed to run VMs
cp bin/safeagent ~/.local/bin/     # or anywhere on your PATH
```

 

**2. Connect it to Claude Code.**

```bash
safeagent claude install
```

This shows the three hooks it will add to `~/.claude/settings.json`
(`WorktreeCreate`, `WorktreeRemove`, `SessionStart`), keeps a backup, and
asks which folders to turn safeagent on for. safeagent only ever acts in those
folders; everywhere else, worktrees stay plain worktrees.

 
 Or use the Claude Code plugin instead 

The plugin carries the same three hooks (and a small script that finds the
`safeagent` command), and nothing else. In any Claude Code session, from any
folder:

```text
/plugin marketplace add skerrysoft/safeagent
/plugin install safeagent@safeagent
```

The first command adds this GitHub repository as a plugin marketplace; the
second installs the plugin for your user, in every project. safeagent itself
must still be installed (step 1), and it still only acts in the folders you
enable (`safeagent enable DIR`). Use the plugin or `safeagent claude install`, not
both: two `WorktreeCreate` hooks would both try to make the worktree.

 

**3. Start sessions in worktrees, as you already do.**

```bash
claude --worktree fix-login
```

or turn on **Worktree** when starting a session in the Claude desktop app.
Subagents and background sessions that use worktrees work the same way.

That's all. Optionally, show each workspace in Claude Code's status line, so
you can see it being prepared (add to `~/.claude/settings.json`):

```json
"statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "safeagent statusline" }
```

**Without Claude Code** (or with another agent), make a workspace yourself
and work in it:

```bash
safeagent enable ~/code              # once: safeagent acts only in folders you enable
cd ~/code/shop
safeagent plan                       # what safeagent found, before anything runs
cd "$(safeagent create fix-login)"   # a worktree that gets its own VM
safeagent exec -- npm test           # the first command boots and prepares it, then runs
safeagent start                      # run the project's apps, forwarded to your machine
safeagent status                     # services, apps, and where each is on your machine
```

## What happens in a session

1. **Claude creates the worktree through safeagent.** In an enabled folder it
 becomes a *workspace*; elsewhere, a plain worktree, made the way Claude
 would make it.
2. **The session opens right away**, and safeagent prepares the workspace in
 the background: builds or reuses the VM image, boots the VM (about half a
 second), starts the services (Postgres, Valkey, Temporal), creates the
 databases, installs dependencies, builds, and runs the setup you
 configured. The first time for a project this takes a minute or two;
 after that, seconds. So the database is there when you run migrations
 or tests.
3. **Nothing waits on that but the commands that need the VM.** Claude can
 read and edit code and use git meanwhile. A command that needs the VM
 (`npm test`, say) waits for it, printing each step, and the status line
 shows where preparation has got to.
4. **Commands go to the right place automatically.** `node`, `npm`, `npx`,
 `yarn`, `pnpm` and `corepack` run in the VM, as do the commands of any
 other runtime the project lists (`python`, `go`, …). Everything else,
 git included, runs on your machine with your keys and settings. Claude is
 told how the workspace works when the session starts.
5. **Your apps start when you start them, not before.** Preparing a
 workspace never runs the project's own apps (its API, web app,
 workers). When your change is ready to try, run `safeagent start` (all of
 them) or `safeagent start web` (one, with the library watchers it needs),
 or ask Claude to. They run in the VM, restart if they crash, and are
 forwarded to your machine; `safeagent stop` stops them, and so does the
 VM stopping (`safeagent down`, or 30 minutes unused). Running your own
 dev command (`npm run dev`) works too: it runs in the VM like any
 other.
6. **Removing the worktree removes the workspace**: its VM and its data.
 Uncommitted work and branches with commits are never deleted.

## How it works

- **One VM per workspace**, on Apple's Virtualization framework: a small
 Linux kernel (Alpine's) and a userland built from signature-verified
 Wolfi packages, shared read-only by every workspace
 that needs the same runtimes and services. It boots in about half a
 second.
- **Your checkout, live.** The worktree is shared into the VM at the same
 path (virtio-fs), so your editor, git and the VM all see the same files.
 Dependencies install into it as Linux builds.
- **Its own disks.** Service data (Postgres, Valkey) and caches (the home
 directory, `/tmp`) live on sparse disk images of the workspace's own;
 the rest of the system is in memory.
- **A guest agent**, the VM's first process, runs the services and apps
 and takes commands from safeagent over SSH on vsock, with keys pinned per
 workspace.
- **A user-mode network.** The VM's network card connects to a network
 stack inside safeagent (gVisor's), which lets it reach
 the internet and nothing local. Ports are forwarded to your machine's
 `127.0.0.1`.
- **Sized to the project**: 4 CPUs and 3 GB by default, more memory for
 each service and app, within half your machine.

## Configure a project

Most projects need no configuration. safeagent reads the files a project
already has:

| Service | Started when the project has… | Commands in the VM get |
|---|---|---|
| `postgres`: PostgreSQL 17 with pgvector and the contrib extensions | `pg`, `postgres`, `pg-promise` (npm); `pgx`, `lib/pq` (Go); `psycopg`, `asyncpg` (Python); `pg` (Ruby); a `postgres`/`pgvector` image in a compose file | `DATABASE_URL`, `PG*`; database `app`, with `vector` installed |
| `valkey`: Valkey 8 (Redis-compatible) | `redis`, `ioredis`, `bullmq`, `iovalkey` (npm); `go-redis`, `valkey-go`; `redis` (Python, Ruby); a `redis`/`valkey` image | `REDIS_URL`, `VALKEY_URL` |
| `temporal`: Temporal dev server | `@temporalio/client` or `/worker`; `go.temporal.io/sdk`; `temporalio` (Python); a `temporalio/*` image | `TEMPORAL_ADDRESS` |

It also installs dependencies from the lockfile (`npm ci`,
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync --frozen`, …), reads every
package of a monorepo, gives each new workspace copies of your checkout's
local `.env` files (so apps run as they do in your checkout), creates the
local databases they point to, and builds what the apps import. safeagent
itself reads env files only for local addresses, ports and variable
names: every other value, and any password in a URL, is dropped as the
file is read, and nothing from them is stored, printed or sent anywhere.
It also finds the project's apps (packages with a `dev` script and a
port, Procfile processes, Django's and Rails' dev servers), which
`safeagent start` runs, with their ports forwarded to your machine; they
never start on their own. `safeagent plan` shows all of it before anything runs,
including how each app is wired: what in the VM answers at every local
address its env files name, and what nothing does. To say exactly what a
workspace needs, add a `safeagent.yaml` at the repository root:

```yaml
services: [postgres, temporal]
runtimes: [python@3.12]        # Node is always there
packages: [ffmpeg]             # extra packages, by name
setup:                         # in the VM, in order, when the data is new
  - npm ci
  - npm run migrate
apps: [api, web]               # what `safeagent start` runs
ports: [3000]                  # forward another port to your machine
```

Setup runs once for a workspace's data, and again when its inputs change
(dependencies, migrations, `safeagent.yaml`). **The `safeagent.yaml`
reference** explains every key and exactly what runs
when, in which order.

The services' variables are set for every command in the VM, so they win
over the same names in a `.env` file (dotenv loaders don't override
variables that are already set). `safeagent status` shows the services and the
ports they are forwarded to on your machine; `safeagent url postgres` prints a
URL, password included, for tools such as `psql` or a database GUI.

## Working with git

The checkout is never copied into the VM. Your worktree stays an ordinary
folder on your machine; the VM sees the same folder, live, at the same
path, through a shared file system. Git runs on your machine, not in the
VM, so it works as it always does:

- **Rebase, merge, pull, switch branches** in the worktree as usual
 (`git pull --rebase origin dev`, `git merge dev`). The VM sees the new
 files the moment git writes them.
- **New dependencies or migrations arrive with a merge?** The next command
 that runs in the VM notices (safeagent watches lockfiles, migration folders
 and `safeagent.yaml`) and runs setup again first, so the workspace installs
 them and migrates its own database.
- **A rebase rewrote migrations the database already ran?** Start the
 data over: `safeagent reset` (back to the snapshot, if the repository has
 one, else empty), and setup migrates it from scratch.
- **Your editor, git GUI and Claude's file tools** all work on the same
 files on your machine; paths in errors and stack traces match.

Code in the VM can't redirect your git: the worktree's `.git` pointer is
locked, and repositories or Claude Code settings planted in the checkout
are quarantined (see Security).

## Data: seeds and snapshots

A workspace can start with real data, migrated for its own branch. A dump in
the repository loads in `safeagent.yaml` (`seed: {postgres: db/seed.sql.gz}`);
a dump that isn't (an anonymized copy of production, say) loads from your
machine:

```bash
safeagent reset --empty && safeagent seed ~/dumps/prod.dump   # in one workspace
safeagent snapshot save                                    # make it the default
```

Every new workspace of the repository then starts from that snapshot (on
macOS, an APFS clone: instant, and taking no space until it changes) and
runs its own branch's setup on top. `safeagent reset` goes back to the
snapshot; `safeagent snapshot ls` and `safeagent snapshot rm NAME` manage them.

Snapshots and `safeagent reset` cover service data only. What commands keep
in the VM's home directory and `/tmp` (package caches, downloaded
browsers, build output) lives on a second disk of the workspace's own, so
it doesn't take the VM's memory; the home directory keeps it across
restarts, and `/tmp` starts empty. It is never in a snapshot,
`safeagent reset` leaves it, and removing the workspace deletes it.

## Security

Workspaces run untrusted code: dependencies' install scripts, repository
scripts, and whatever an agent decides to run. safeagent is built to contain
it. Found a way out? Please report it privately, as
SECURITY.md describes.

**What protects you**

- **VM boundary.** Each workspace is a Linux VM (on macOS, Apple's
 Virtualization framework, which runs each VM in its own sandboxed
 process). It sees only its checkout, the read-only system image and its
 own configuration, never your machine's other files.
- **A network that only goes out.** A VM's network card connects to a
 user-mode network stack inside safeagent, not to a bridge or your machine's
 network. Every connection is checked after DNS resolution: public
 addresses are allowed; loopback, private and link-local ranges (cloud
 metadata included), carrier-grade NAT, multicast, your machine's own
 addresses and every network it is directly attached to (VPNs included)
 are refused, as is outgoing mail (port 25). A VM can hold at most 512 TCP
 and 128 UDP flows, so it can't exhaust your machine's ports. DNS goes
 through your machine's resolver. Refused connections are logged
 (`safeagent logs network`).
- **Services reachable only from your machine.** Forwarded ports listen on
 `127.0.0.1` only, at ports safeagent picks (never ones the checkout names,
 which could take over ports your own servers use). From your machine,
 Postgres and Valkey each require their own password, which other local
 users can't read; services without a password aren't forwarded unless
 you ask. The apps' web ports answer only to `localhost` names, so a web
 page can't reach them by DNS rebinding.
- **Trust inside the VM only.** Inside the VM, where everything runs as
 root anyway, Postgres trusts the user a command names, so a project's
 `.env` URLs work unchanged (on other ports too, which relay to the
 service inside the VM). Connections forwarded from your machine never
 get that trust.
- **Clean output.** What safeagent prints from the VM (logs, errors) is
 stripped of terminal control sequences.
- **Locked git metadata.** The worktree's `.git` pointer is made immutable,
 and safeagent's own git commands name the repository explicitly, so a VM
 can't redirect them. After every command, at session start and every
 15 seconds while a VM runs, safeagent scans the checkout for planted
 repositories and Claude Code settings and quarantines them.
- **Opt-in.** Nothing happens outside folders you enable. Creating a
 worktree never runs the repository's filter drivers, or its hooks unless
 you opt in.
- **Pinned keys.** Host and VM authenticate each other with per-workspace
 SSH keys that safeagent generates. Nothing is trusted on first use.
- **Verified images.** Every package is checked against a signed index
 (Wolfi's and Alpine's pinned keys) down to each file, extraction can't
 write outside the image directory, and install scripts run in a build VM.
- **Careful deletion and bounded logs.** safeagent only deletes worktrees it
 created, never a branch that holds commits, and caps the logs a VM can
 write on your disk.

Each of these is tested by attacking a real VM from the inside
(scripts/escape-test.sh), and the parsers that read
VM or repository input are fuzzed.

**Known gaps**

- The checkout is shared read-write: that is how your edits reach the VM and
 its output reaches you. Code in the VM can change your source files, and
 files git tracks under `.claude/`. Review changes as you would any
 dependency's.
- Something running in the background in a VM could plant a file between
 scans (up to 15 seconds).
- No disk quota yet: a VM can fill the disk through its checkout, and its
 service data disk and its home disk (caches) can each grow to 64 GB.
 Space the VM frees is handed back to your machine.
- The Temporal dev server and its UI have no authentication. If you forward
 them, any process of any user on your machine can reach them.
- A web page served from a VM and opened in your browser is a local page: it
 can send requests to other services on your machine's loopback interface,
 as any local web app can. Open workspace apps through their `*.localhost`
 URLs.
- A snapshot's data reaches every new workspace of its repository, whatever
 branch it is on, and code in those VMs can reach the internet. Don't save
 data in a snapshot that you wouldn't give to every branch you check out
 (an outside contributor's included).
- Setup commands from `safeagent.yaml`, dependency installs and builds run
 in the VM without asking, as `npm install` would; the project's apps run
 when you (or Claude) run `safeagent start`.
- Your local `.env` files (secrets included) are copied into each new
 workspace, as Claude Code's `.worktreeinclude` copies what it lists, so
 code in the VM can read them, and the VM can reach the internet. Add a
 `.worktreeinclude` to choose exactly which files a workspace gets.
- A VM can reach anything public, from your machine's public address: code
 in it can send what it can read (the checkout) to the internet, and reach
 services that trust your IP address or a public range routed over your
 VPN. An allowlist mode is planned.
- No external security review yet.

The full threat model, and the rules every change is tested against, are in
docs/design.md.

## Commands

You rarely need these with Claude Code; these are the ones for working by
hand:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `safeagent plan [--env] [DIR]` | Show what safeagent would set up for a checkout, and how its apps are wired, without starting anything |
| `safeagent create NAME [--base BRANCH]` | Make a workspace (worktree on branch `worktree-NAME`) and print its path |
| `safeagent start [APP…]` / `stop [APP…]` | Run or stop the project's apps in the VM (all, or the ones named); they never start on their own |
| `safeagent status [NAME]` | Preparation, services, setup, whether each app answers, and where everything is on your machine |
| `safeagent exec -- CMD…` | Run a command in the workspace's VM |
| `safeagent logs [-f] WHAT` | A service's or an app's output, or `setup`, `console`, `network` |
| `safeagent rm NAME [--force]` | Remove a workspace; `--force` discards uncommitted changes but never a branch with commits |

Commands that act on a workspace use the one you're in, unless you name one.

 
 All commands and settings 

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `safeagent claude install` / `uninstall` | Add or remove the Claude Code hooks |
| `safeagent enable [DIR]` / `disable [DIR]`, `enable --list` | Turn safeagent on or off for a folder and everything under it |
| `safeagent ls` | List workspaces |
| `safeagent up [NAME]` / `down [NAME]` | Start (and prepare) or stop a workspace's VM |
| `safeagent url [-w NAME] SERVICE` | Print a URL for a service, password included, for tools on your machine |
| `safeagent setup [NAME]` | Run the project's seed and setup again |
| `safeagent seed [-w NAME] FILE` | Load a `.sql`, `.sql.gz` or `.dump` file into the workspace's empty Postgres |
| `safeagent snapshot save [S]` / `ls` / `rm S` | Save the workspace's data for new workspaces (`default`); list or delete snapshots |
| `safeagent reset [NAME] [--snapshot S \| --empty]` | Start the workspace's data over |
| `safeagent gc` | Delete images and downloads no workspace needs |
| `safeagent statusline` | One line for Claude Code's status line |

Settings, through environment variables for now:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `SAFEAGENT_IDLE_STOP` | Stop a workspace's VM after it has been unused (no commands, no connections to its ports) this long (default `30m`; `off` never), apps included. Its data stays; the next command starts it again, and `safeagent start` the apps |
| `SAFEAGENT_CPUS`, `SAFEAGENT_MEMORY` | CPUs and memory per VM (default 4 and `3g`, more memory for each service and app; at most all CPUs and half the machine's memory) |
| `SAFEAGENT_BASE=head` | Start new worktrees at your current commit instead of the remote's default branch |
| `SAFEAGENT_GIT_HOOKS=1` | Let the repository's git hooks run when creating worktrees (off by default) |
| `SAFEAGENT_BRANCH_PREFIX` | Prefix for new branches (default `worktree-`) |
| `SAFEAGENT_FILE_EVENTS=off` | Don't forward file changes to watchers in the VM (by default, watchers in a VM see edits made on your machine) |
| `SAFEAGENT_SHIMS=off` | Run your machine's own `node`, `python`… even in workspaces |
| `SAFEAGENT_HOME` | Keep all of safeagent's state and caches under one directory |

 

## What works today

| | |
|---|---|
| ✅ Claude Code hooks: CLI, desktop app, subagents, background sessions; plugin | verified |
| ✅ One VM per workspace on macOS (Apple Silicon) | ~0.5 s boot |
| ✅ Preparation in the background, with progress in the status line and `safeagent status` | |
| ✅ Networking: internet yes; your machine, local network and cloud metadata no | |
| ✅ Services: Postgres 17 + pgvector, Valkey, Temporal; data kept per workspace | |
| ✅ Runtimes: Node, Python, Go, Ruby, Java, Bun, Deno; extra packages by name | |
| ✅ Dependencies installed from the lockfile; setup re-run when a merge changes them | |
| ✅ Monorepos: services, apps and library watchers detected across packages; `safeagent start` runs apps with forwarded ports | |
| ✅ Procfiles, Django and Rails dev servers; Python, Ruby and Go runtimes detected | |
| ✅ Local `.env` files copied into workspaces; the databases they name created; their secrets never read | |
| ✅ Seeds, setup commands (migrations), snapshots cloned per workspace | |
| ✅ Hot reload; idle stop; CPU and memory limits | |
| ✅ Images built only from signature-verified packages | |
| 🚧 Linux hosts | in progress |

## Building from source

- macOS on Apple Silicon (built and tested on macOS 27); Go 1.27+ and git
- Network access the first time an image is built: packages come from Wolfi
 (packages.wolfi.dev) and the kernel from Alpine. About 100 MB, more with
 services and runtimes.

`make build` builds the guest agent for Linux, embeds it in `bin/safeagent`, and
signs `bin/safeagent` with the `com.apple.security.virtualization` entitlement
so it can start VMs. A plain `go build` produces a binary without the agent
or the signature.

## Feedback

safeagent is early. If it gets something wrong on your project (a service it
missed, an app it didn't find, setup that failed), `safeagent plan` output in
an issue helps most.
Security problems go to SECURITY.md instead.

title: Show HN: Cassandra – free tool to check if you got affected by the Cursor hack
author: skd-fs
body:
Cassandra 
by 
How it works 
 Advisories 
Check your machine for the Claude Code backdoor.
One command. Read-only, no sudo, nothing sent. Yes, it is a script that looks for a script,
 so the whole thing is on this page . Read it, then run it.
macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://ciphero.ai/cassandra.sh | bash Copy 
Windows, in PowerShell
irm https://ciphero.ai/cassandra.ps1 | iex Copy 
Prefer not to pipe? curl -fsSL -o cassandra.sh https://ciphero.ai/cassandra.sh && less cassandra.sh && bash cassandra.sh 
What it does
Looks for the indicators in Cursor's notice for the Claude Code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 backdoor: the svc-telemetry SSH key and the two key fingerprints, the com.apple.sysmond LaunchAgent, the tunnel files in ~/.config , the cron line, the SysMon task and sysmon.cmd , the attacker IP. In the places the notice names, and in the places the same thing could sit under another name: shell start-up files, other LaunchAgents, units and tasks, the Run key, the process list, open connections, the code of your other extensions. 19 checks in all (13 apply on macOS, 11 on Linux, 12 on Windows). Cursor's own one-liner covers the first.
Hashes extension.js inside any installed Claude Code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 and greps it for the attacker strings, which tells a genuine copy from the backdoored one. Greps the editor's install log and removed-extensions list for either version, for the common case: the bad build was installed on Oct 29 and an update has since replaced it.
Prints found or clear per check and ends with one of these:
■ NO TRACES None of the 13 published indicators were found on this machine.
■ BAD VERSION WAS INSTALLED In the editor's install history: cursor:anthropic.claude-code-2.1.313.
 → Treat the machine as exposed: rotate the keys and tokens it used, from another machine.
■ TRACES FOUND 2 of 13 published indicators were found on this machine.
 → Treat it as compromised. Steps, per incident: /advisories 
Why more than Cursor's grep
Cursor's check is one grep: svc-telemetry in authorized_keys , and "machine not impacted" when it is absent. That settles whether the key is there now. It leaves three things open, and they are what the script was written for.
The backdoor is more than the key. By the notice's own account the tunnel failed on most machines, for want of admin rights, and the key, the persistence and the beacon went ahead regardless. The persistence is a LaunchAgent, a scheduled task or a startup script that retries the tunnel every 60 seconds, and it survives uninstalling the extension and deleting the key by hand. The script checks the persistence, the tunnel files and key, the cron line, the Run key, the process list and open connections, and the same places under other names.
Whether you ever had the bad build. Cursor auto-updates extensions. If 2.1.313 was replaced by 2.1.314 later that day, the extension folder is clean, the grep can be clean, and the beacon still went out on Oct 29 with your hostname, username, environment variable names, Git email and public IP. The notice's step 2 is to search your extension-installation telemetry; most people have none. The editor's own install log and removed-extensions list are that telemetry for one machine. The script reads them: that is the BAD VERSION WAS INSTALLED ending, and why it says rotate.
Whether an installed copy is the bad one. A version number is not the answer; the notice publishes the hash of the modified extension.js and the two strings inside it. The script hashes the file and greps it, and reports a backdoored build as such.
Then
Traces found, or the backdoored build installed: disconnect the machine, rotate SSH keys, cloud and API credentials and Git tokens from a different machine, run Cursor's remediation script. Steps on the advisory .
Bad version was installed, nothing else found: the update removed the extension, not what it did while installed. The beacon went out, and the notice says what it took does not rule out later credential access. Rotate the credentials this machine used, from another machine.
This is one incident. The script finds what has been published about it and nothing else: an extension nobody has flagged yet, a poisoned npm or pip package, a malicious MCP server or model file are all out of its reach. The full check adds Ciphero's known-malicious database and the marketplaces, which cover the extensions, and that is still the whole of it.
Nothing found: you are clear of this incident's published indicators. Update Claude Code to 2.1.314 or later if you have not.
Want the rest? The full check is this script with a real token: after you type yes, it also matches your extension ids against Ciphero's database of thousands of known-malicious ones and the marketplaces, and emails a report. That is why it asks for an address first. Free. Not needed for this incident.
Before you run it

# Cassandra · malicious extension check · by Ciphero
#

# Firefox and others), by folder name: id and version only. If a

# extension's main file and greps it for the published attacker

# a genuine copy of the version is told from the backdoored one.
# 2. Checks a fixed list of places (below): named files and folders,
# your shell start-up files, your own crontab, your LaunchAgents,
# systemd units and autostart entries, the running process list

# specific incidents. It records yes / no plus the name of what
# matched (a file name, an extension folder). It sends no file
# contents and no paths, only the answer.
# 3. Lists AI tool names and the NAMES (never values) of API-key variables.
# 4. Shows you every fact it will send and asks before sending.
# 5. Sends them to Ciphero over HTTPS. Ciphero matches the extensions
# against known-malicious lists and the marketplaces, and prints
# your risk level.
#

# Run it only on a machine you own or are allowed to check. By sending

# and privacy policy (https://ciphero.ai/privacy#cassandra).
# Incidents it looks for traces of:

# https://cursor.com/blog/claude-code-extension-security-notice
#

}

say " ${B}Ready to send ${NFACTS} facts to Ciphero.${R} ${D}No file contents, no key values.${R}"
say " ${D}Sending accepts Ciphero's terms and privacy policy: https://ciphero.ai/terms#cassandra${R}"
ANSWER=""
while :; do
 if [ "${CASSANDRA_YES:-}" = 1 ]; then ANSWER=y
 elif (exec < /dev/tty) 2>/dev/null; then
 printf ' Send them? [y]es / [n]o / [s]how every line: ' > /dev/tty
 read -r ANSWER < /dev/tty || ANSWER=n
 else say " No terminal to ask on. Re-run with CASSANDRA_YES=1 to send without asking."; exit 1; fi
 case "$ANSWER" in
 s|S|show) printf '%s' "$OUT" | sed 's/^/ /' ;;
 n|N|no|No|NO) say " Nothing sent."; exit 0 ;;
 y|Y|yes|Yes|YES) break ;;
 *) say " ${D}Please answer y, n or s.${R}" ;;
 esac
done
RESP="$(printf '%s' "$OUT" | curl -fsS --max-time 40 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' --data-binary @- "$CASSANDRA_URL" 2>&1)" || {
 say " ${RED}Upload failed:${R} $RESP"; exit 1; }
say ""
printf '%s\n' "$RESP" | while IFS='|' read -r level text; do
 case "$level" in
 critical) say " ${RED}${B}■ CRITICAL${R} ${B}$text${R}" ;;
 high) say " ${AMB}${B}■ HIGH${R} ${B}$text${R}" ;;
 caution) say " ${YEL}${B}■ CAUTION${R} ${B}$text${R}" ;;
 clear) say " ${GRN}${B}■ CLEAR${R} ${B}$text${R}" ;;
 step) say " ${GLD}→${R} $text" ;;
 error) say " ${RED}${B}■${R} $text" ;;
 *) say " ${D}$text${R}" ;;
 esac
done
say ""
}

 # Cassandra - malicious extension check - by Ciphero
#
# Lists the extensions installed in your editors (VS Code, Cursor,
# Windsurf and other forks) and browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Firefox
# and others) by folder name: id and version only. If a version an
# incident below names is installed, hashes that extension's main file
# and checks it for the published attacker strings (the hash and a
# yes / no go, never the file). Checks a fixed list of places (named
# files and folders, your Run keys, the scheduled tasks, the running
# processes and the code of your other extensions) for the traces of
# specific incidents: yes / no plus the name of what matched, never
# file contents. Lists AI tool names and the NAMES (never values) of
# API-key variables, shows you every fact, asks before sending, then
# prints your risk level. Ciphero matches the extensions against
# known-malicious lists and the marketplaces. Installs nothing.
# Run it only on a machine you own or are allowed to check. By sending
# the facts you accept Ciphero's terms (https://ciphero.ai/terms#cassandra)
# and privacy policy (https://ciphero.ai/privacy#cassandra).
# Incidents it looks for traces of:
# CSA-2026-0001 - Malicious Claude Code extensions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 (Cursor marketplace)
# https://cursor.com/blog/claude-code-extension-security-notice
#
# The readable copy at https://ciphero.ai/cassandra.ps1 is this same file with
# YOUR-CHECK-TOKEN in place of a check token. Run as is, it does every
# check, prints its own summary of the incident traces and stops before
# asking to send: it has no token, so there is nothing it can send to.
#
# Cmdlets only, no .NET calls beyond strings and hashtables, so it also
# runs under Constrained Language Mode on managed machines. Its state
# lives in one hashtable ($cx) rather than in your session's variables.
& {
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'SilentlyContinue'
 $ProgressPreference = 'SilentlyContinue'
 $url = 'https://ciphero.ai/cassandra/scan/YOUR-CHECK-TOKEN'
 $token = 'YOUR-CHECK-TOKEN'
 $cx = @{ facts = @(); checkId = ''; extDirs = @(); extCount = 0; bextCount = 0; bseen = @{}; bnames = @(); checks = 0; found = 0; backdoored = @(); history = @() }
 $psNoise = @('PSPath', 'PSParentPath', 'PSChildName', 'PSDrive', 'PSProvider')
 function Add-Fact { $cx.facts += ($args -join "`t") }
 function Show-Row($label, $st) {
 switch ($st) {
 'yes' { Write-Host " * $label " -NoNewline; Write-Host 'found' -ForegroundColor Red }
 'no' { Write-Host " o $label " -NoNewline -ForegroundColor DarkGray; Write-Host 'clear' -ForegroundColor Green }
 'na' { Write-Host " . $label n/a" -ForegroundColor DarkGray }
 default { Write-Host " ? $label " -NoNewline; Write-Host 'could not check' -ForegroundColor Yellow }
 }
 }
 # A file under ProgramData that this user can't open (OpenSSH Server's
 # administrators_authorized_keys) is one that code running as this user
 # couldn't have written either: not applicable, not a failed check.
 function Test-AdminOnly($p) {
 if (-not $env:ProgramData) { return $false }
 if (-not $p.ToLowerInvariant().StartsWith($env:ProgramData.ToLowerInvariant())) { return $false }
 try { $null = Get-Content -LiteralPath $p -TotalCount 1 -ErrorAction Stop; return $false } catch { return $true }
 }
 # Each probe returns yes / no / na / err and records the name of
 # what matched (a file, a key, an extension folder): never a path
 # under the profile, never contents. A wildcard sits only in the last
 # segment of a path, so it expands as a filter inside its literal
 # parent folder; brackets elsewhere in the path stay literal.
 function Add-Hit($name) { Add-Fact 'hit' $cx.checkId $name }
 function Expand-Paths($paths) {
 $found = @()
 foreach ($p in $paths) {
 if ($p -match '[*?]') {
 $dir = Split-Path $p -Parent; $leaf = Split-Path $p -Leaf
 if ($dir -and (Test-Path -LiteralPath $dir)) {
 $found += @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $dir -Filter $leaf -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object { $_.FullName })
 }
 } elseif (Test-Path -LiteralPath $p -PathType Leaf) { $found += $p }
 }
 return $found
 }
 function Test-Contains($needle, $paths) {
 $st = 'no'; $read = $false; $skipped = $false
 foreach ($p in (Expand-Paths $paths)) {
 if (Test-AdminOnly $p) { $skipped = $true; continue }
 try {
 if (Select-String -LiteralPath $p -SimpleMatch -Pattern $needle -Quiet -ErrorAction Stop) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit (Split-Path $p -Leaf) }
 $read = $true
 } catch { if ($st -ne 'yes') { $st = 'err' } }
 }
 if ($st -eq 'no' -and $skipped -and -not $read) { return 'na' }
 return $st
 }
 function Test-Fingerprint($needle, $paths) {
 $st = 'no'; $read = $false; $skipped = $false
 $keygen = Get-Command ssh-keygen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
 foreach ($p in (Expand-Paths $paths)) {
 if (Test-AdminOnly $p) { $skipped = $true; continue }
 if (-not $keygen) { $st = 'err'; continue }
 # Empty input on stdin: ssh-keygen -l asks nothing, and if a build
 # ever did, it gets an answer instead of waiting on the terminal.
 $fp = '' | & ssh-keygen -lf $p -E sha256 2>$null
 if (-not $fp) { continue }
 if (($fp -join ' ').Contains($needle)) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit (Split-Path $p -Leaf) }
 $read = $true
 }
 if ($st -eq 'no' -and $skipped -and -not $read) { return 'na' }
 return $st
 }
 function Test-Any($paths) {
 $st = 'no'
 foreach ($p in $paths) {
 if ($p -match '[*?]') {
 $dir = Split-Path $p -Parent; $leaf = Split-Path $p -Leaf
 if ($dir -and (Test-Path -LiteralPath $dir)) {
 foreach ($f in @(Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $dir -Filter $leaf -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit $f.Name }
 }
 } elseif (Test-Path -LiteralPath $p) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit (Split-Path $p -Leaf) }
 }
 return $st
 }
 # The user's own Run keys: persistence the notice did not list.
 function Test-RunKey($needle) {
 $st = 'no'
 foreach ($k in 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run', 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce') {
 $props = Get-ItemProperty -Path $k -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
 if (-not $props) { continue }
 foreach ($p in $props.PSObject.Properties) {
 if ($psNoise -contains $p.Name) { continue }
 if ("$($p.Value)".Contains($needle)) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit $p.Name }
 }
 }
 return $st
 }
 # Any scheduled task whose action runs the needle, whatever the task is called.
 function Test-TaskAction($needle) {
 if (-not (Get-Command Get-ScheduledTask -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) { return 'err' }
 $st = 'no'
 foreach ($t in @(Get-ScheduledTask -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
 foreach ($a in @($t.Actions)) {
 if ("$($a.Execute) $($a.Arguments)".Contains($needle)) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit $t.TaskName; break }
 }
 }
 return $st
 }
 # The needle inside the code of any installed extension other than
 # the versions an incident already names. Top-level, dist and out
 # scripts only (a few MB at most), so it stays fast.
 function Test-ExtCode($needle) {
 $st = 'no'
 foreach ($pair in $cx.extDirs) {
 $editor, $dir = $pair
 foreach ($f in @(Get-ChildItem -Path "$dir\*\*.js", "$dir\*\dist\*.js", "$dir\*\out\*.js" -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
 if ($f.Length -gt 64MB) { continue }
 $folder = (($f.FullName.Substring($dir.Length) -replace '^[\\/]+', '') -split '[\\/]')[0]
 $named = $false
 foreach ($n in $needles) { if ($folder.StartsWith($n)) { $named = $true } }
 if ($named) { continue }
 if (Select-String -LiteralPath $f.FullName -SimpleMatch -Pattern $needle -Quiet -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) { $st = 'yes'; Add-Hit "${editor}:$folder" }
 }
 }
 return $st
 }
 function Test-Task($name) {
 if (Get-Command Get-ScheduledTask -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
 if (Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -eq $name }) { return 'yes' } else { return 'no' }
 }
 schtasks /Query /TN $name *> $null
 if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { return 'yes' } else { return 'no' }
 }
 function Test-Connection2($ip) {
 if (Get-Command Get-NetTCPConnection -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
 if (Get-NetTCPConnection -RemoteAddress $ip -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) { return 'yes' } else { return 'no' }
 }
 if (netstat -an | Select-String -SimpleMatch $ip) { return 'yes' } else { return 'no' }
 }
 function Test-Process($needle) {
 $procs = Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
 if (-not $procs) { return 'err' }
 foreach ($p in $procs) { if ($p.CommandLine -and $p.CommandLine.Contains($needle)) { return 'yes' } }
 return 'no'
 }
 # A check's status is the last yes / no / na / err its probe
 # returned; anything else a cmdlet let slip into the pipeline is
 # ignored, and a probe that throws is 'could not check'.
 function Run-Check($id, $label, $probe) {
 $cx.checkId = $id
 $st = 'err'
 try {
 $seen = @(& $probe) | Where-Object { "$_" -in @('yes', 'no', 'na', 'err') } | Select-Object -Last 1
 if ($seen) { $st = "$seen" }
 } catch { $st = 'err' }
 Add-Fact 'check' $id $st; Show-Row $label $st
 $cx.checks += 1; if ($st -eq 'yes') { $cx.found += 1 }
 }
Write-Host ''
 Write-Host ' CASSANDRA' -ForegroundColor DarkYellow -NoNewline; Write-Host ' malicious extension check by Ciphero' -ForegroundColor DarkGray
 Write-Host ''
 $mode = "$($ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode)"
 if ($mode -and $mode -ne 'FullLanguage') {
 Write-Host " PowerShell runs in $mode here, a policy on this machine. Cassandra is written for it; anything it cannot check will say so." -ForegroundColor DarkGray
 Write-Host ''
 }
 Add-Fact 'v' '3'
 Add-Fact 'os' 'windows'
 Add-Fact 'arch' $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE
 Add-Fact 'host' $env:COMPUTERNAME
$needles = @('anthropic.claude-code-2.1.312', 'anthropic.claude-code-2.1.313')
 function List-Exts($editor, $dir) {
 if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $dir)) { return }
 $cx.extDirs += ,@($editor, (Get-Item -LiteralPath $dir).FullName)
 Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $dir -Directory -Force | Where-Object { -not $_.Name.StartsWith('.') } | ForEach-Object {
 Add-Fact 'ext' $editor $_.Name; $cx.extCount += 1
 }
 $obs = Join-Path $dir '.obsolete'
 if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $obs) {
 $text = Get-Content -LiteralPath $obs -Raw
 foreach ($n in $needles) { if ($text -and $text.Contains($n)) { Add-Fact 'hist' $editor $n 'obsolete'; Note-Hist $editor $n } }
 }
 }
 # editor:version pairs the install history names, for the readable
 # copy's own summary (the full check's verdict gets the facts).
 function Note-Hist($editor, $n) { if ($cx.history -notcontains "${editor}:$n") { $cx.history += "${editor}:$n" } }
 # The editor's own install log names the versions it installed and
 # removed: a second history source for a version an update replaced.
 function Log-History($editor, $dir) {
 if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $dir)) { return }
 $logs = @(Get-ChildItem -Path "$dir\*\main.log", "$dir\*\sharedprocess.log" -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)
 foreach ($n in $needles) {
 foreach ($f in $logs) {
 if (Select-String -LiteralPath $f.FullName -SimpleMatch -Pattern $n -Quiet) { Add-Fact 'hist' $editor $n 'logs'; Note-Hist $editor $n; break }
 }
 }
 }
 function Vsix-Cache($editor, $dir) {
 if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $dir)) { return }
 Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $dir -File | ForEach-Object {
 $f = $_
 foreach ($n in $needles) {
 if ($f.Name.StartsWith($n)) { Add-Fact 'vsix' $editor $f.Name ((Get-FileHash -LiteralPath $f.FullName -Algorithm SHA256).Hash.ToLower()) }
 }
 }
 }
 # The main file of an installed copy of a version an incident names:
 # its SHA-256, and whether

title: Show HN: An open source repo to use your personal context with any agent
author: symuz
body:
Memex
How it works Dreaming Your data GitHub 
Open source. Work in progress.
Your repo remembers the code. Memex remembers you.
The durable context about you and your work, like preferences, decisions and background, shouldn't live inside one AI app. Keep it in your own database and let any agent use it.
Hi agent, set up Memex for me. Follow the instructions in SETUP.md at https://github.com/predsymod/memex 
 Copy 
Paste that into any coding agent. It walks you through the setup and does the typing for you.
In Claude, on Monday
save to memex: my favorite color is red 
Saved to Memex.
kept in your own database
In Muse, on Friday
hi, sync memex
One new note from Claude. Pulled.
what's my favorite color?
Red. You saved that from Claude on Monday.
What goes in Memex
The durable, cross-cutting context that every tool should know, and that no single repo can hold.
Keeps 
 What follows you
Your preferences and how you like to work, decisions and the reasons behind them, corrections, people and plans, and stable background on your products and projects.
Leaves to the repo 
 What lives with the code
Code-specific context, status updates and to-dos stay in your repo, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md . Agents are told to leave them out of Memex.
Three things you say
Memex is an MCP server that runs on your own Supabase project. Agents connect to it, and the instructions they follow are plain text in the repo.
Setup 
 Point an agent at the repo
It creates the tables, deploys the server and connects itself. You approve the steps that need an account.
"Set up Memex. Follow SETUP.md in the repo."
Sync 
 One memory, every agent
An agent pushes what it knows that is worth keeping and pulls what the others learned, without duplicates. You decide, for each agent, what it may save.
"Sync memex."
Invoke 
 Use it in your work
Search blends meaning with exact words, favors recent notes when you ask, and shows the current version of anything that was corrected.
"Review memex, then draft the plan."
Hands-off, if you want it
Ask any agent that can run scheduled tasks to keep you in sync. Say it once, and every morning it catches up on what your other agents saved and, if you choose, saves what it learned.
Pull only 
 Stay current
"Sync memex every morning at 7."
Fetches what your other agents saved and gives you a short summary. Nothing is saved, so nothing needs approving.
Pull and save 
 Stay in sync
"Sync memex every morning and save what's worth keeping."
Your yes at setup is the standing approval. Each run it saves a few durable decisions, lessons and facts, and tells you exactly what it saved.
Built so it stays safe while you're not watching. The server itself caps an unattended run at a small number of short notes (10 by default, and you can change it), skips anything that looks like a secret, skips repeats of what it already saved (or what you retracted), and tags every note it saves. Agents are told to leave out anything taken from web pages or emails. If a save was wrong, "retract what you saved this morning" hides those notes, and only those, and they can be restored. Nothing is ever deleted.
How the pieces fit
No hosted service in the middle. The server and the database both live in your own Supabase project. 
Dreaming, if you turn it on
A nightly job reads what you saved since the last run and organizes it. It never deletes or rewrites what you wrote. Everything it changes is logged and can be undone.
Tags, summaries and types for every memory, with relative dates like "next Friday" turned into real dates.
Connections between memories: related, elaborates, supersedes, duplicate.
Corrections win. When a later note corrects an earlier one, the old one is marked superseded, ranks lower in search, and the current version is shown next to it. If an agent later saves the old fact again, it is flagged as disputed and the correction is shown first.
Overviews. When enough notes pile up about one topic, Dreaming writes a single note of the current picture: what it is, what was decided, where it stands. It's linked back to its sources and rewritten when new notes join.
A short digest of what changed.
115 notes, 40 seconds one pass over a real personal memory 
Under $1 for that first pass; pennies a day after 
Off by default it only runs if you add a model API key 
Your data, your keys
Memories live in your own Supabase database. There is no Memex server run by anyone else.
Costs are pennies a month: a small embeddings charge per memory, plus Dreaming if you turn it on.
Anything that looks like a secret (keys, tokens, card or ID numbers) is flagged, never sent to a model, and hidden from search and sync.
Agents are told to treat memories as evidence, never as instructions.
One thing to know: memories are sent to an embeddings provider so they can be searched by meaning, and to a model provider if you enable Dreaming. You choose the providers, and the repo says exactly what is sent.
Works with
Tested with Claude and Muse, reading and writing the same memory. Any agent that supports MCP over HTTP should work: Codex, Cursor, VS Code and others connect with a URL and a key.
Memex is building on the excellent Open Brain project by Nate B. Jones, and on an earlier write-up, Liberating memory . Source and setup instructions are on GitHub .

title: Show HN: Phonon TTS on WebGPU, 44MB, 115x real time, with live word timings
author: blixt
body: I tried Gradium's Phonon 31M text-to-speech model and was blown away by its quality to size ratio. I needed timings for every word to be able to highlight them, so I wrote a second runtime for it with a different design: the whole generation loop stays on the GPU in WebGPU kernels written specifically for this by Claude Opus 5.5.When initialized, it can start streaming audio in about 3 ms, and it only needs to download 44 MB (<40 MB brotli'd) instead of the official 67 MB, because every large matrix is stored as int8, the audio decoder included. On the same devices it runs at 115x real time vs. 31x on my M3 Max, and 26x against 13x on my iPhone 17 Pro. The timings are read from one of the model's attention heads while it speaks, so we practically get the time offsets of words for free.Demo: blixt.xyz/phononCode and benchmarks: github.com/blixt/phononGradium did an amazing job on this model, and I'm still wrapping my head around that you can get realtime human-sounding speech from a 40 MB file on a website.

title: Show HN: Cppbolt – A lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust
author: ajtimepyro
body:
Hey HN! I've been working on cppbolt, a lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust.The idea was to build something that can compile and run C++ directly in the browser without downloading a massive LLVM/Clang toolchain.Unlike projects that bundle LLVM/Clang and can require 100+ MB of compiler assets, cppbolt's compiler payload is around 1 MB. It compiles a supported subset of C++17 directly to standard WebAssembly binaries.Some things it supports:
- Classes, inheritance, virtual functions and operator overloading
- Templates and a subset of the C++ standard library
- Pointers, references, arrays and dynamic memory
- Lambdas, structured bindings and range-based loopsIt comes with a browser playground, CLI and npm package.A few caveats: this is still a work in progress, it doesn't implement the full C++17 standard, and it might not work as expected with certain C++ programs. I'm particularly interested in feedback on the compiler architecture, language support and potential use cases and also interested in connecting with someone who might want to use it in their application.Try it out:
- Playground: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/
- Docs: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/book/
- GitHub: https://github.com/AJTimePyro/cppbolt
- npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cppboltWould love to hear what you think, especially from people who've worked on compilers or WebAssembly.

With so many existing C++ projects and optimized code, being able to convert them is highly useful.Just curious, have you tried to open a cpp project and use a tool like Claude to just convert it to WebAssembly and compare? That would make a great data point if you can show that cppbolt can do it much better/faster.

title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
author: schopra909
body:
My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation.Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling.When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace.Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task.This serves 3 purposes:
1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training)
2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart)
3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality)This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples.We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website.For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

title: Show HN: GPUWorks – A 40 MB GPU cluster manager for vLLM/SGLang, no K8s needed
author: wangweinoo1
body:
# flitai-io/gpuworks A ~45 MB MaaS platform: one cluster across public and private clouds, on any mix of accelerators. - Stars: 64 - Forks: 24 - Watchers: 64 - Open issues: 2 - License: Apache License 2.0 - Default branch: master - Created: 2026-10-22T22:17:35Z ## Languages - C - CSS - Dockerfile - Go - HTML - JavaScript - Makefile - Python - SCSS - Shell - TypeScript ## Top Contributors - MatheMatrix (613 contributions) - AlanJager (343 contributions) - Kid-G0629 (3 contributions) - yahuuu (3 contributions) --- ## README A 40 MB MaaS platform: one cluster across public and private clouds, on any mix of accelerators. English | 简体中文 GPUWorks is an ultra-lightweight GPU management and Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) platform. The whole control plane, web UI included, is a 40 MB download. Join your own GPU servers, rented cloud instances or containers, or a Mac with one command, pick a model, and GPUWorks estimates the memory it needs, picks the GPUs, starts vLLM, SGLang or any engine an inference template defines (Strata, ninfer, …), and serves it behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. NVIDIA, AMD Instinct and Ryzen AI Max, Huawei Ascend, T-Head PPU, Hygon DCU and Apple Silicon run side by side in the same cluster. The pool of capacity is the core: bare-metal servers, public cloud instances and private cloud VMs today, with Kubernetes clusters and Slurm partitions joining next. On top of it, GPUWorks serves models now and will run fine-tuning and training jobs on the same accelerators. ## Highlights - **Verified model × accelerator combinations deploy in one click.** The built-in catalog ships 1,235 launch specs for 392 models: image, engine, flags and pinned weight revisions for each GPU type. The combinations we have run on real NVIDIA, AMD, Ascend, PPU and Apple hardware come with launch settings that are known to work, so you pick a model and press deploy instead of hunting for flags. Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, Llama, Gemma, gpt-oss, plus embedding, rerank, speech, image and video models. - **Heterogeneous accelerators, one scheduler.** NVIDIA, AMD, Ascend, PPU, Hygon and Apple Silicon nodes join the same cluster; the scheduler matches each deployment to hardware its launch spec supports. - **Public and private cloud in one pool.** Sync instances from RunPod, CompShare, AutoDL, Vast.ai and Alibaba Cloud, or VMs from ZStack Cloud, install the agent in one click, and schedule them together with your own servers. - **Ultra-lightweight.** The server and the agent are each one static binary (`CGO_ENABLED=0`); the server embeds the web UI (English / 中文) and the agents for every platform, and keeps its state in one SQLite file. The agent dials out over WebSocket, so nodes need no inbound ports (or the server dials in, for nodes that cannot reach out). In a drill on Alibaba Cloud, one server ran 1,003 rented GPU machines across 7 regions: over 500 replicas placed and running within 4 minutes, and 2,000 concurrent requests through the gateway with the server peaking at 9 CPU cores and 1.6 GB of memory. - **Memory estimate and explained placement.** Before anything starts, you see how much GPU memory weights, KV cache and engine overhead need, which GPUs the scheduler picked and why the others were rejected. - **Share a GPU between models.** dGPU puts a hard memory quota on each instance so several models fit on one card (NVIDIA via HAMi-core, Ascend via vCANN, PPU via HGGC, Hygon via hy-smi virtual devices). Sleep/wake lets vLLM models take turns on the same GPUs on NVIDIA, Ascend, PPU and Hygon. - **Scale out.** Replicas across nodes, multi-node tensor/pipeline parallel, and prefill/decode disaggregation (vLLM + NIXL on NVIDIA, vLLM-Ascend + Mooncake on Ascend, SGLang or vLLM + Mooncake on PPU, within one host or over RDMA, and experimental vLLM + Mooncake on Hygon). - **OpenAI-compatible gateway.** Chat, completions, embeddings, rerank, audio, images, video and realtime under `/v1`; `/v1/messages` and `/v1/responses` pass through. Least-request, prefix-affinity or failover routing, API keys, per-key token usage. - **See what is going on.** GPU and engine metrics, searchable logs, per-request traces with a timeline (OTLP export), a web terminal into hosts and containers, and a built-in benchmark that sweeps concurrency and finds the SLA limit. - **AI assistant and MCP.** Ask questions about the cluster in the UI, or connect Claude Code / any MCP client to the read-only MCP endpoint. - **Air-gapped ready.** Import images and models from archives or an HTTP file server, and sync models between nodes. ## Quick start **1. Install the server** on a Linux host (x86_64 or arm64) or an Apple Silicon Mac: ```bash bash <(curl -fsSL https://dl.gpuworks.ai/get.sh) ``` The script picks the fastest download source (including mirrors in mainland China), verifies the checksum and runs the installer, which sets up a service on port 8800 and prints the URL and the admin password. Add `--quiet` to accept every default. To check each step yourself, follow the manual install. **2. Add a GPU node.** Open the web UI, go to **Compute nodes → Add node**, and run the generated command on the GPU host: ```bash curl -fsSL http://:8800/install.sh | sh -s -- --server http://:8800 --token ``` **3. Deploy a model.** Open **Deploy**, pick a model such as `Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B` and a recommended inference template, review the configuration evaluation (memory estimate and placement), and deploy. Then create an inference token under **API Tokens** and call the model by its public model name: ```bash curl http://:8800/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer gw-..." -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model": "qwen3-1.7b", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]}' ``` The full walkthrough is in Getting started. For a Mac, see Run your first local model on a Mac; for air-gapped sites, see Offline deployment. ### Install with an AI coding agent Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or a similar agent that has shell access to your server: ```text Install the GPUWorks control plane on this host and verify it. 1. Run `bash <(curl -fsSL https://dl.gpuworks.ai/get.sh) --quiet`. It downloads the latest build, verifies its checksum and installs a service on port 8800 (use sudo when asked). If I have no sudo or no systemd, append `--dir ~/gpuworks-server --no-systemd` instead. 2. Verify with `curl -fsS http:///healthz` (expect "status":"ok") and show me the install summary: URL, install directory, data directory and the initial admin password location. 3. Do not open firewall ports, change other services, or join GPU nodes. Tell me which address GPU nodes should use to reach the server; I will add nodes from the web UI. ``` ## Supported hardware | Accelerator | Whole-GPU deploy | dGPU (shared GPU) | Sleep/wake | Multi-node | PD disaggregation | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **NVIDIA** (CUDA) | ✅ Docker, containerd or runveil (built-in rootless runtime) | ✅ memory quota at MiB granularity | ✅ vLLM | ✅ | ✅ vLLM + NIXL | | **AMD** (ROCm: Instinct MI300 series, Ryzen AI Max) | ✅ Docker, containerd or runveil (built-in rootless runtime) | ✅ memory quota (libvrocm, user space) | ✅ vLLM | ✅ vLLM | ✅ vLLM + NIXL | | **Huawei Ascend** (CANN) | ✅ Docker, containerd or runveil (built-in rootless runtime) | ✅ memory quota at MiB granularity | ✅ vLLM-Ascend | ✅ | ✅ vLLM-Ascend + Mooncake | | **T-Head PPU** (HGGC) | ✅ Docker, containerd or runveil (built-in rootless runtime) | ✅ memory quota at MiB granularity | ✅ vLLM | ✅ | ✅ SGLang + Mooncake (same node or over RDMA), vLLM + Mooncake (RDMA) | | **Hygon DCU** (DTK) | ✅ Docker, containerd or runveil (built-in rootless runtime) | ✅ memory quota at MiB granularity | ✅ vLLM | ✅ | 🧪 vLLM 0.21 + Mooncake | | **Apple Silicon** (M1–M5, macOS 15+) | ✅ vllm-metal, MLX, llama.cpp as native processes | — | — | — | — | ✅ verified on real hardware · 🧪 experimental · — not supported or not validated. Sleep/wake beyond NVIDIA is verified on Ascend 910C, PPU ZW810E, Hygon K100 and AMD MI300X; the tested versions and limits are in choosing features. GPUs are detected with the vendor CLIs (`nvidia-smi`, `npu-smi`, `ppu-smi`, `hy-smi`) or, for AMD, amdgpu sysfs and KFD, so there is no NVML or cgo dependency. Per-combination status lives in the support matrix and the Ascend matrix. **Engines:** vLLM (incl. vLLM-Ascend and vLLM-Omni), SGLang, and on Mac vllm-metal, MLX-VLM, MLX-Audio and llama.cpp. Built-in images are published as `gpuworks/gpuworks-runner` on Docker Hub, Quay and Huawei SWR (image families); you can also bring your own image. ## Model catalog The built-in catalog pins every model to fixed Hugging Face and ModelScope revisions and ships launch specs per engine and accelerator. The deploy page recommends the specs that match the model and the target accelerator. | Type | Examples | |---|---| | Chat / reasoning / code | Qwen3 / 3.5 / 3.6 / 3.8, Qwen3-Coder, DeepSeek R1 / V3.2 / V4, GLM-4.5 – 5.3, Kimi K2 – K3, MiniMax M2 – M3, Llama 3.x / 4, Gemma 3 / 4, gpt-oss, Mistral Large 3, ERNIE 4.5, Step-3.5, MiMo, Seed-OSS, Nemotron | | Vision-language / OCR | Qwen3-VL, Qwen3-Omni, GLM-4.xV, Kimi-VL, DeepSeek-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, GLM-OCR | | Embedding / rerank | Qwen3-Embedding, Qwen3-Reranker, bge-m3, bge-reranker-v2-m3, Jina v5, EmbeddingGemma | | Speech | Qwen3-ASR, Whisper large-v3, Qwen3-TTS, GLM-TTS, Voxtral, FishAudio S2-Pro | | Image / video | Qwen-Image, GLM-Image, Stable Diffusion 3.5, Wan 2.1 / 2.2, LTX-2.5, Cosmos3 | Catalog totals: 392 models from 77 organizations, 1,235 launch specs (745 NVIDIA, 216 PPU, 209 Ascend, 41 Hygon, 15 AMD, 9 Apple). Models outside the catalog can be registered from Hugging Face, ModelScope, a local directory, NFS or an HTTP file server and deployed with your own arguments. ## Screenshots | | | |---|---| | Overview **Overview** of a production cluster with NVIDIA, PPU, Ascend and Hygon GPUs | Scheduling **Scheduling analysis**: models taking turns on the same GPUs, card by card | | Monitor **Monitoring** in production: latency, request shapes, concurrency and KV cache over 7 days | Usage **Usage analytics**: tokens by hour, API key and model | | PD **PD disaggregation** on Ascend 910C: KV hand-off, latency breakdown, requests in flight | Health **GPU health checks**, diagnosed by the AI assistant | | Network **Network test**: HCCS card-to-card reachability matrix | Benchmark **Benchmark** report: throughput, TTFT, latency | | Templates **Model catalog** with launch specs per vendor and engine | Playground **Playground** against any deployment | ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR user["Browser / CLI / MCP client"] -->|"Web UI, REST API"| server app["Apps (OpenAI SDK)"] -->|"/v1/* + API key"| server subgraph server["gpuworks server (one binary)"] direction TB gw["OpenAI gateway"] ctl["Controller + scheduler
memory estimate"] db[("SQLite
metrics · logs · traces")] end subgraph node1["GPU node"] a1["gpuworks-agent"] --> e1["vLLM / SGLang
Docker · nerdctl · runveil"] end subgraph node2["Mac"] a2["gpuworks-agent"] --> e2["vllm-metal / MLX / llama.cpp"] end a1 -->|"outbound WebSocket + yamux
ctrl lane / data lane"| server a2 -->|"outbound WebSocket"| server ``` - The **server** is the control plane: REST API and web UI, the OpenAI-compatible gateway, a controller that reconciles desired state, the scheduler, and storage for metrics, logs and request traces. - An **agent** runs on each GPU node. It probes the accelerators, runs engines through Docker, nerdctl, the built-in rootless runtime (runveil) or as host processes on macOS, and reports metrics and logs. - Agents connect out to the server and multiplex everything over two lanes: `ctrl` for commands, metrics and terminals, `data` for inference traffic, logs and model/image transfer. Inference requests reach the engine through that tunnel, so nodes never expose ports. More in Architecture and the ADRs. ## Documentation | I want to… | Go to | |---|---| | Get it running | Getting started · Install the server · Connect nodes | | Fit more on my GPUs | Choosing features · dGPU · Sleep/wake · Two models on one GPU | | Serve bigger models or more traffic | Multi-node inference · PD disaggregation · Scale replicas | | Measure and debug | Benchmark · Monitoring and logs · Trace a slow request · Troubleshooting | | Integrate | OpenAI gateway · REST API · MCP · CLI | | Run it in production | Production checklist · Offline · Upgrades · Security | Everything else: documentation index. Documentation Website ## Build from source Requires Go 1.26 and Node.js. ```bash make build # web UI + server + agents into ./bin make demo # throwaway server + a GPU-less agent: onboarding, heartbeat, reconnect make test # static checks + Go unit tests + UI tests make test-l2 # multi-process tests with real binaries and fake GPUs ``` See the developer docs and testing guide. How to file a report, send a patch, or get a hardware combination into the support matrix is in CONTRIBUTING.md; contributor conventions are in CLAUDE.md (Chinese) and domain terms in CONTEXT.md. Security issues go to SECURITY.md — never a public issue. ## Help us improve the product Production installations send one anonymous usage report per day (hardware and engine mix, task counts, error categories; no hostnames, model inputs or outputs, or any other sensitive information). Turn it off in **Settings → General** or with `usage_report: false` in `server.yaml`. Every field is listed in User Experience Improvement Program. ## License GPUWorks is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. Bundled third-party components keep their own licenses; see NOTICE. # YashwanthKamireddi/Skykeep

title: Show HN: 25posts – Guess the impressions of real LinkedIn posts
author: bilyas509
body: I have been posting on LinkedIn for more than 18 months and have had more than 4 million impressions.The one thing it took me a while to understand is that there is not a single algorithm.My belief is that the number of impressions highly depends on the one posting.I made a web game based on this thesis.You are shown real posts and have to guess the number of impressions.I find it quite entertaining, but it also questions our beliefs about how platforms like LinkedIn and X work.I will be available to answer all your questions and would be happy to hear your thoughts on the gameplay.

Your iCloud, at home on Linux and Windows: Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Contacts, iCloud Drive and Photos as real desktop apps on a native Rust engine. Instant, offline, in sync with your iPhone. Free and open source.
